A wasted opponent round only raises the survivors' level, so a split that reserves a few hundred knock-out rounds instead meets the bound against every opponent and is the version worth learning from.
problems.statement_summary: In an interactive, adaptive game with at most fifty cups, one player repeatedly distributes at most a fixed number of litres of milk tea among cups, after which opponents empty a window of consecutive cups of a fixed length, at most ten. He may instead end with a last distribution nobody drinks, and within two thousand rounds must guarantee some cup holds essentially the largest amount any strategy can force.
problems.review_rationale: I checked the value independently: with u survivors at common level v the quantity v + x*H_u is invariant under pour-x/u-and-lose-one, the levelling phase ends with m-1 slots at x, and the final free pour gives x*(1 + H_{m-1}); m = 2 gives the fixed point 2x by direct minimax and m = 3 matches the value iteration, and the disjoint-block adversary makes the m-slot game an upper bound on any pouring strategy. game-theory stands: the students genuinely choose (adaptive interactor), the target is a minimax value proved by a potential function, and the corpus already uses the label for non-combinatorial adversarial problems such as codeforces-1427-h. constructive-algorithm at 0.7 follows the corpus norm for interactive strategy-design carriers (7 of 10 sampled). On the wasteful-opponent shortfall: it is a note, not a blocker for publication, because the labels and summary describe the problem and the accepted approach, and Kattis accepted this code; but the code is genuinely not adversary-proof, since each wasted opponent round raises every survivor by x/u, so a strategy that reserved roughly 250 knock-out rounds instead of 99 would reach OPT against any opponent within the 2000-round cap, and the 1900/99 split is the only reason the leftmost-window opponent wins.
issues: The solution text presents the published 1900/99 round split as if it guaranteed OPT; it does not against non-minimising opponents (0.73-0.77 of OPT at k = 1, n >= 47). Recommend one added sentence: a robust split reserves a few hundred knock-out rounds, since a wasted opponent round only raises the survivors' level and the invariant then exceeds OPT.
The reference value is judged to 1e-3 relative and the code lands exactly on OPT with zero margin; that is fine for annotation but worth knowing if anyone reuses the code as a reference.

problems.solution: Choosing the problem set means picking x easy, y medium and z hard proposals with 1 <= x <= a, 1 <= y <= b, 1 <= z <= c and x + y + z = n. Such a triple exists exactly when a, b and c are all at least 1 (so one of each is available) and 3 <= n <= a + b + c: the minimum reachable total is 3 and the maximum is a + b + c, and every total in between is reachable because raising one coordinate at a time changes the sum by one. The answer is therefore the single test a >= 1 and b >= 1 and c >= 1 and 3 <= n <= a + b + c, evaluated in O(1); with a, b, c <= 10 and n <= 20 the equivalent triple loop over at most 11^3 candidates is also well within limits. Both samples reproduce, and the closed form was checked against the brute force over the entire input space (all 11 * 11 * 11 * 20 inputs) with no mismatch.
problems.statement_summary: A committee has collected a easy, b medium and c hard problem proposals and wants to assemble a set of exactly n problems that contains at least one problem of each of the three difficulties. Given the four integers, where each pool holds at most ten proposals and n is at most twenty, the task is to report whether such a selection is possible.
problems.review_rationale: Closed form a,b,c >= 1 and 3 <= n <= a+b+c is right (contiguity of the reachable sums is immediate) and the script's exhaustive sweep of the whole 11^3*20 input space passed on my run. I rule to keep brute-force at 0.5 rather than emptying the list: the six existing single-brute-force corpus entries are exactly this kind of tiny-bound div2-A problem, the 11^3 triple loop is a genuinely common accepted solution, and the only empty-patterns entry in the corpus is a special/joke problem, so an empty list would be the outlier. No other label is defensible; greedy/counting/constructive were rightly refused.
issues: Sub-0.6 label kept by precedent (19 such labels already in the index); if the index later enforces a 0.6 floor this entry should carry [] rather than an inflated confidence.

problems.solution: If i = p1^q1 * ... * pm^qm then i has exactly (q1+1)...(qm+1) divisors of which exactly m are prime, so NPF(i) = d(i) - omega(i), where d counts divisors and omega counts distinct prime divisors; that identity reproduces all four samples (100 -> 9-2 = 7, 13 -> 2-1 = 1, 12 -> 6-2 = 4, 2018 -> 4-2 = 2). Both tables are precomputed once for every value up to 2*10^6 by sieving rather than per query: the harmonic loop 'for each d, bump a counter at every multiple of d' gives d(i) in O(M log M), and the same loop restricted to primes gives omega(i) in O(M log log M) -- equivalently, skipping the primes in the first loop accumulates NPF directly. Each query is then a single array lookup, so the whole program is O(M log M + Q) time and O(M) memory; NPF never exceeds 283 on this range, so a 16-bit table of 2*10^6 entries (4 MB) is enough. The deciding constraint is the query count: with Q up to 3*10^6 and i up to 2*10^6, per-query trial division costs about 240 divisions on average and up to 1400 for a prime, so roughly 5*10^8 divisions in total even when memoised over the at most 2*10^6 distinct inputs, too slow for the 1 s limit, and the sheer I/O volume forces buffered or unformatted reading and writing.
problems.statement_summary: For each of up to three million queries the task is to report how many divisors of a given integer are not themselves prime, where that integer is at least two and at most two million. Because the queries greatly outnumber the distinct possible inputs and the input and output volume is very large, an answer must be produced in effectively constant time per query.
problems.review_rationale: NPF(i) = d(i) - omega(i) is correct and reproduces the samples; the harmonic sieve is O(M log M) build plus O(1) per query with a 4 MB 16-bit table, which is the only approach comfortably inside Kattis's 1 s limit (fetched: 1 second, 1024 MB). Re-ran verify_nonprimefactors.py: tables match trial-division factorisation up to 2*10^5 and explicit divisor enumeration up to 2*10^4. The claim that the slides' per-query trial division would not pass is directionally right at 1 s but overstated as written, see issues. prime-factorization at 0.6 is kept: the identity is a statement about the factorisation and the common SPF-sieve implementation does factorise.
issues: Solution text says per-query trial division 'costs about 1400 steps' and is 'far too slow even when memoised'. 1400 is the prime-input worst case; I measured the average over random i <= 2*10^6 at about 240 iterations for naive trial division and about 48 when dividing by primes only, so memoised over 2*10^6 distinct inputs that is roughly 4.8*10^8 versus 1*10^8 divisions. At the 1 s limit the naive form the slides describe is indeed too slow, but the primes-only form is borderline rather than hopeless. Recommend rewording to 'about 240 divisions on average, up to 1400 for primes; roughly 5*10^8 in total even when memoised, too slow for the 1 s limit'. Not blocking: the chosen solution and its limits claim are correct.

problems.solution: f is an iterated morphism (a D0L system): every letter c is rewritten as the fixed word T_c, and since every |T_c| >= 2 the expansion of a single letter after k rounds has length at least 2^k. Because every queried position is at most 10^15 < 2^50, at any level deeper than 50 the position is forced to lie inside the expansion of the FIRST character, so the top K-50 steps of the descent are the deterministic map g(c) = first letter of T_c, a functional graph on 26 nodes; folding it by rho/cycle detection (tail plus cycle is at most 26) yields g^(K-50)(S[0]) in O(26) time, which replaces S by that one letter and K by 50. With K' = min(K,50) the lengths L[k][c] = |f^k(c)| are then built bottom-up with saturating addition capped just above 10^15 (so the true value is recovered exactly whenever it is below the cap, which is all the descent ever compares against), one prefix pass over S decides which letter of S owns each query, and each query walks down at most 50 levels, scanning the at most 50 children per level to find the one containing the remaining offset. The whole answer for a query is thus read off without ever materialising the string, and the per-query work is bounded because the fold above level 50 is forced rather than chosen. Time is O(|S| + 26*K'*maxT + M*K'*maxT), about 3 million operations at |S| = 10^6, K = 10^15, M = 1000, and space is O(|S| + 26*K') for the prefix sums and the small length table.
problems.statement_summary: A password starts as a lowercase string of up to a million letters and is grown by simultaneously replacing every letter with a fixed word assigned to that letter, each word at least two letters long, repeating that substitution as many as a quadrillion times. For up to a thousand forgotten positions, none beyond a quadrillion, the task is to report which letter stands at each of those positions.
problems.review_rationale: The 50-level fold is correct: |T_c| >= 2 gives |f^k(c)| >= 2^k and 2^50 > 10^15, so at every level with at least 50 expansions remaining the query lies in the first letter's image and the top K-50 steps are iterates of the first-letter map on 26 nodes, which needs cycle detection (10^15 steps cannot be simulated). Below that, saturating lengths plus a 50-level descent scanning at most 50 children per level answers each query; O(|S| + M*50*50) time and O(|S|) space fit. Samples and 400 random cross-checks against literal expansion (342 exercising the fold) passed on my run. functional-graph and cycle-detection are the genuine techniques; binary-search/prefix-sum/offline-queries were rightly treated as scaffolding. The vocabulary lacks the actual shape (k-th leaf descent of an iterated morphism), which the notes record.
issues: The debrief text extraction is lossy (matrix layout, '1015'); the reconstruction is verified independently so this is a provenance note only.

problems.solution: The given hash is H(prev,T,tok) = (v*7 + tok) mod p with p = 1e9+7, where v is the polynomial-31 hash of the transaction string seeded with prev. The token enters linearly with coefficient 1, so there is no search at all: fix any transaction string T, compute v, pick a target of the form k*1e7 (the valid hash values are the 100 positive multiples of 1e7 that are at most p-1), and the required token is forced as tok = (target - 7v) mod p. The only side condition is tok <= 1e9-1, which excludes just the 7 residues 1e9..1e9+6, so trying successive targets finds one immediately. Do this once to forge block A from the input hash, then again with A's hash as prev to forge block B, giving O(|T|) total work.
problems.statement_summary: A blockchain block is valid when a specified polynomial hash of the previous block's hash, a transaction string and a token yields a positive value with seven trailing zeros modulo 1000000007. Given the current last hash, the task is to output two chained blocks, printing a transaction string and token for one appended to it and for a second appended to that, each token below one billion.
problems.review_rationale: Checked the algebra: H = (7v + tok) mod p with tok entering linearly, so tok = (target - 7v) mod p is forced for any of the 100 positive multiples of 10^7 below p, and only the 7 residues in [10^9, 10^9+6] are excluded, so a valid target always exists. Re-ran verify_sgcoin.py: reproduces all four H values printed in the statement (including the 140000000 -> 930000000 -> 730000000 chain) and forges valid two-block chains for 2004 inputs; O(|T|) time, O(1) space. Nothing is mined, so constructive-algorithm plus modular-arithmetic is the right pair and string-hashing/brute-force are correctly withheld.

problems.solution: Root the target tree at the pre-placed block. Every legal history keeps the placed set connected and containing the root, because each new block must touch an existing one, so the placed set is always a root-closed subtree; hence the neighbour a new block bumps into can never be one of its children (a child's own path to the root would run through the still-absent block), and must be its parent. That pins each block's move exactly: it enters from the edge opposite its parent, travelling along its own row when the parent is horizontally adjacent and its own column otherwise, and it imposes two ordering constraints - the parent goes first, and the block itself goes before every target block on the ray from it to its entry edge. Those constraints are both necessary (just shown) and sufficient (following any order that respects them, each block finds its parent present and its ray clear, so it stops exactly where it must), so the answer is any topological order of the constraint digraph and impossibility is precisely a cycle, detected by Kahn's algorithm. Writing the ray constraints out is quadratic in the number of blocks, so every row and column gets prefix and suffix chains of auxiliary nodes and a block points at one chain node standing for its whole ray, keeping the graph at O(B) nodes and edges. Sorting blocks along rows and columns dominates, giving O(B log B) time and O(B) space, and the board is never materialised, which matters because N and M reach 4*10^5 while only B cells are occupied.
problems.statement_summary: A board starts with one block, and a move injects a new block from one of the four edges along a chosen row or column; it slides until it bumps into an existing block, and a move adding nothing is illegal. Given a target arrangement of up to four hundred thousand blocks whose cells form a tree under adjacency, the task is to decide reachability and list the moves.
problems.review_rationale: Re-ruled after the coordinator's edit: patterns are now exactly topological-sort, graph-modeling, constructive-algorithm, with dfs and cycle-detection removed from both fields and a SKEPTIC EDIT sentence in notes; the older 'Label notes' sentence about them now reads as the reason they were dropped. The central claim was independently confirmed: the NUS debrief says verbatim 'we only need to add edges from block u to the next block in that direction', my own implementation of that rule on the 7x4 board emits a move list that replays to a board with a block at (1,2) and none at (6,2), and my own 2^B BFS shows the target is reachable, so the debrief's reduction gives wrong answers. The characterisation and the prefix/suffix chain repair are sound, O(B log B) time and O(B) space with the grid never materialised fit the fetched 4 s; verify_slidingblocks.py passes samples, 6000 random boards and 270 dense maximal trees against the BFS with every move list replayed. Approved as it now stands.

problems.solution: Only extremal occurrences matter: if indices c<d<e<f witness A,B,A,B, then replacing c by the last occurrence of A before d and e by that occurrence's immediate successor, and f by the last occurrence of B anywhere, still leaves a witness, so the ordered pair (A,B) is achievable exactly when some index u lies strictly between two CONSECUTIVE occurrences p<q of A and the last occurrence of the value at u is beyond q. That turns the whole search into one range-maximum query per occurrence-gap over the array IM[i] = last occurrence of S[i], and the gaps number N-1 in total across all values, so a sparse table (or the debrief's event-sorted segment tree over the same reduction) answers each in O(1) after an O(N log N) build. The smallest achievable A is then the smallest value owning a gap whose IM-maximum exceeds that gap's right end, and for that single A one linear scan of the span from its first to its last occurrence, carrying the next occurrence of A, yields the smallest qualifying B - which is the part the debrief never addresses, since it argues existence only and the problem actually demands the lexicographically smallest pair. Correctness of the reduction is the two-line exchange argument above in both directions; a witness quadruple maps to such a (p,u,q) triple, and any such triple is itself a witness. Cost is O(N log N) time and O(N log N) space for the sparse table, or O(N) space if a segment tree is used instead, which clears N = 400000 comfortably (0.5 s in plain Python on the worst shapes tried). Verified on all three samples, against exhaustive O(N^4) quadruple search on 40000 random sequences with small alphabets, and against an independent cubic reference on 400 longer ones plus adversarial single-value-spanning shapes.
problems.statement_summary: A message is a sequence of up to four hundred thousand positive integers, none larger than the length of the sequence. The task is to decide whether some two distinct values appear in the repeating order A, B, A, B as a not necessarily contiguous subsequence, and if so to report the lexicographically smallest such ordered pair, otherwise to report that no such pair exists.
problems.review_rationale: Re-ruled after the coordinator's edit: patterns are now exactly segment-tree, sparse-table, lexicographic-order, with line-sweep and offline-queries removed from both patterns and pattern_confidence and a SKEPTIC EDIT sentence in notes recording why; the surviving 'Label caveats' sentence reads as history, not as a claim, so it is fine. The solution itself was already verified: the 2-page NUS debrief (text-extracted) decides existence only and never mentions the lexicographically smallest pair; the consecutive-occurrence reduction is correct in both directions; smallest A by a gap-RMQ test then one linear scan of A's span for smallest B is right; O(N log N) time and about 30 MB of sparse table at N=4*10^5 fit the fetched 2 s / 1024 MB; verify_wiknow.py passes samples, 40000 exhaustive-brute cases, 400 cubic-reference cases and spanning shapes. Approved as it now stands.

problems.solution: A simple path from B to G through C splits at C into two paths B->C and G->C that share no cell except C, and conversely, so the shortest such path is the minimum total length of two such vertex-disjoint paths. Split each cell into in and out nodes joined by a capacity-1 arc (capacity 2 for C), delete U, give each grid step cost 1, feed one unit into B and one into G from a super source and drain 2 units out of C. Costs are non-negative so no cycle appears in the flow and the two units decompose into the wanted paths; infeasible means NO, and the path string is read off the flow. Two Dijkstra augmentations with potentials give O(NM log(NM)) per test, fine for total NM <= 1e5.
problems.statement_summary: On a grid of at most one hundred by one hundred cells, a walker must travel from a start cell to a goal cell by unit steps, passing through a third marked cell somewhere on the way and never entering a fourth forbidden cell, and no cell may be visited twice. The task prints a shortest such route as a string of directions, or reports that none exists.
problems.review_rationale: I re-derived the reduction rather than trusting it: a simple path B->G through C is exactly a pair of paths B->C and G->C meeting only at C, in/out arcs of capacity 1 (2 at C) enforce vertex-disjointness, U is deleted, and non-negative unit costs mean the value-2 min-cost flow contains no cycle and decomposes into exactly those two paths; flow value below 2 is Menger's certificate for NO. Limits are comfortable rather than tight: the sum of N*M is 1e5, so the entire input is at most 2e5 split nodes and two Dijkstra augmentations per test, O(NM log NM) time and O(NM) memory. The second unit cannot sneak back through C because the in-out arc there has total capacity 2 and the sink is only reachable through it.
issues: verify_amazingadventures.py compares only the min-cost flow VALUE against brute force; it never reconstructs or validates the U/D/L/R direction string that the problem actually requires, and the largest grid it tests is 4x4. Path reconstruction is mechanical, but the output-format half of the solution is entirely untested.

The proposal's notes hedge that a direct case analysis may exist and 'would make some of these labels secondary'. That hedge stays in the notes and did not leak into the label list, which is the right handling.

problems.solution: Brute force over every bipartite graph with parts up to 5 and 4 shows the Grundy value of the delete-a-vertex-or-an-edge game is exactly ((a+b) mod 2) + 2*(|E| mod 2). Socket, moving second, wins iff the XOR over the N games is 0, i.e. iff sum(a_i+b_i) is even and an even number of graphs carry an odd edge count. The low bit is fixed by the input, so the answer is 0 when sum(a_i+b_i) is odd; otherwise the edge parities are independent and uniform, exactly half of the 2^(a_i b_i) drawings of each graph being odd, so the count is 2^(sum a_i*b_i - 1) mod 1e9+7. O(N log) time with one modular exponentiation, O(1) space.
problems.statement_summary: Two players alternately delete one vertex or one edge from any still non-empty graph among N drawn bipartite graphs, the i-th having parts of a_i and b_i vertices, and whoever cannot move loses. The task counts, modulo 1000000007, the ways to draw the edge sets so that the second player wins under optimal play, with N up to 100000 and part sizes up to 1000000000.
problems.review_rationale: The Grundy claim is checked element by element over every edge set on 15 part-size pairs, not merely by value distribution, and the counting formula is checked against full enumeration on eleven multi-graph inputs; I re-derived both samples by hand (a=b=1 gives Grundy 0 and 2 for the two drawings, hence answer 1; a=1,b=2 has odd a+b hence 0) and they agree. The final algorithm is O(N) plus one modular exponentiation, so time and memory are never in question at N = 1e5, and the halving argument is airtight because a_i*b_i >= 1 always leaves at least one free edge parity. Every label names something the submitted solution actually does, and the brute force that DISCOVERED the Grundy rule is correctly left unlabelled instead of being sold as the route.
issues: The exponent sum(a_i*b_i) reaches about 1e23, so any non-bignum implementation must reduce it mod 1e9+6 by Fermat before the modpow. The write-up says 'one modular exponentiation' without flagging the 64-bit overflow; the Python reference sidesteps it with big ints.
Nit: the summary carries LaTeX-style subscripts 'a_i' and 'b_i'. No brackets or markup, so it passes, but plain words would read better.

problems.solution: Day 1 occupies the N listed cells and every later day adds exactly the cells at edge-distance one from the occupied set, so a cell is taken on day 1 + d where d is its grid distance to the nearest listed cell. Push all N cells into one queue at distance 0 and run a single breadth-first search over the R x C grid; the answer is 1 plus the largest distance reached. Repeated input cells are absorbed by the visited check. O(RC + N) time, O(RC) space, trivially inside R, C <= 100.
problems.statement_summary: An army occupies N given cells of an R by C grid on the first day, and on each later day it also takes every cell that shares an edge with a cell taken earlier. The task reports how many days pass before the whole grid is occupied. The grid has at most 100 rows and 100 columns, and the listed cells need not be distinct.
problems.review_rationale: Day 1 seeds the N listed cells and every later day is exactly one BFS layer, so the answer is 1 plus the eccentricity of the source set; the verify script cross-checks that against a literal day-by-day simulation on 4000 random grids and reproduces both samples including the all-cells-seeded answer of 1. O(RC + N) time and O(RC) memory against R, C <= 100 and N <= 10000 leaves three orders of magnitude of headroom, and duplicate input cells are absorbed by the visited check as the statement warns. All three labels describe what the code does.
issues: Because the grid has no obstacles the answer also equals 1 plus the largest Manhattan distance to the nearest listed cell, so manhattan-distance is a genuine alternative route. I deliberately did NOT add it: it is not the route this solution takes, and adding routes-not-taken is the failure mode this gate exists to catch.

problems.solution: Let f(x) count sprinkles in the half-ring starting at x. Sliding by one part swaps one sprinkle out for at most one in, so f changes by at most 1 per step, and f(x) + f(x+5e8) = N, so g = f - N/2 satisfies g(x+5e8) = -g(x). A discrete intermediate value argument therefore guarantees a zero of g, so the answer NO never happens. One query at x=0 orients an interval of length 5e8 whose endpoints have opposite signs; then binary search, but shrink using the probe value itself (a value v>0 at mid moves the left end to mid+v, v<0 moves the right end to mid+v) since g cannot cross within |v| steps. That reaches a single candidate in at most 28 further queries, so at most 30 interactions, inside the 30 + floor(log2(sqrt(N))) budget even at N=2.
problems.statement_summary: An interactive task on a ring divided into a billion numbered parts carrying N sprinkles, N even. The solver may ask how many sprinkles lie in any circular range of parts, and must name a half of the ring, five hundred million consecutive parts, holding exactly N/2 sprinkles, or report that no such half exists. At most thirty plus floor of log2 of root N interactions are permitted.
problems.review_rationale: I recomputed the interaction budget by hand rather than trusting the harness, because this is the one proposal in the batch where the limit is the difficulty. At N = 2 the budget is exactly 30 including the answer; the search window starts at width 499999998 and each probe takes w to at most ceil(w/2)-1, which reaches width 0 after 28 probes, so 1 orienting query + 28 probes + 1 answer = exactly 30. It fits with zero margin but it does fit. The existence argument is sound: f moves by at most 1 per step and f(x)+f(x+5e8)=N, so g=f-N/2 is antisymmetric under the half-turn and must hit 0, making NO unreachable, which the 4000 simulated runs confirm. Not probing the final L and relying on the invariant is correct, since a positive-to-negative crossing of a step-1 integer function must land on 0.
issues: Zero margin at N = 2 (30 of 30 interactions in the true worst case; the harness happened to observe only 29 because it never hit the exact adversarial configuration). Any extra orienting query at all would fail the judge, so this is the one place an implementation detail could silently break it.

Correctly refused binary-search-answer, and I agree: there is no monotone feasibility predicate here, only a sign change of a function that moves by at most one per step. The value-based shrink (L = mid + v) is an accelerated bisection, not a parametric search.

problems.solution: Every controlled area is a subtree, so the areas containing one berry are nested and its eater is the bird of its label whose area root is deepest; with at most seven birds per label that owner is found by scanning the label's bird list with an Euler-tour ancestor test. Making the tiny birds giant only enlarges areas - subtree(parent) becomes subtree(nearest big ancestor) - so every bird still contains its own berries and the only damage is that a same-label bird may now sit deeper. A berry must keep its eater, hence its label must equal that bird's, so each bird together with the berries it owns forms one block that is relabelled whole or not at all, and since all of them already carry the bird's label the cost of relabelling a block is its size. A relabelled block can always take a brand new label, which clashes with nothing, so the only constraints bind the blocks that KEEP a label L, pairwise: two kept birds of label L must not have equal new areas, and the deeper one must not contain a berry of the shallower one (a binary search over that bird's berries in Euler order). Labels are therefore independent, the 'no eight birds share a label' rule caps a class at seven birds, and the best kept set is the maximum-weight conflict-free subset over all 2^7 subsets; the answer is the total weight minus the kept weight. O(n log n) time, O(n) space.
problems.statement_summary: A rooted tree's internal nodes are big or small; every leaf holds a labelled giant bird, tiny bird or berry. A tiny bird controls its parent's subtree, a giant bird its nearest big ancestor's, and the smallest controlling bird of matching label eats a berry. With every tiny bird turned giant and at most seven birds per label, the fewest labels must change so no berry changes eater.
problems.review_rationale: I re-read the statement against the reduction line by line, since a two-solve problem is usually a reading trap, and every step holds: subtrees containing a common berry are nested so 'smallest controlled area' is unambiguously the deepest root; a tiny bird's parent is either big, in which case the area is unchanged, or small, in which case the nearest big ancestor is a proper ancestor of it, so areas only grow and no bird can lose its own berries; owner preservation forces a berry's label to equal its owner's, making bird-plus-berries an atomic block of cost equal to its size; and a relabelled block can always take a fresh label, of which 12.4 million exist against at most 150000 blocks, so nothing else is disturbed and label classes really are independent. I checked that the pairwise conflict list is complete - the surviving rules after relabelling are equal areas, stolen berries, coverage and the seven-bird cap, and the last two are automatic - and I re-derived all three samples by hand, getting 2, 1 and 0 with sample 2 turning on block WEIGHT rather than block count. O(n log n) and O(n) are right: seven ancestor tests per berry, at most 21 pairs and one 128-subset scan per label, one binary search per pair.
issues: brute-force: I agree with the NO. The algorithm is O(n log n) and the 128-subset scan is a constant-size step inside the reduction, not the method; labelling it would put this record beside genuine search problems.

The 150000-vertex scale run is real, and this is the only proposal in the batch that has one, but it is unrepresentative: the generated instance gives one label 37000 berries and a single bird, every other bird a unique label, so it comes out k = 0 in 0.14s and never exercises a seven-bird class, the conflict enumeration, or the output path. The parse and Euler tour are timed; the interesting half is not.
The 720 random trees top out at 13 vertices. Correctness evidence is strong there (exhaustive over all labellings, plus an independent replay simulator) but there is nothing between 13 and 150000.

Summary nit: it says the fewest labels must change 'so no berry changes eater', which is the headline constraint but not the whole one - the new labelling must also keep the distinct-areas and seven-bird rules. Accurate enough to pass at 68 words.

problems.solution: Fibonacci mod m is purely periodic with period pi(m), so G(k,n) mod m_0 needs G(k-1,n) mod m_1 with m_1 = pi(m_0), and so on down a tower m_0, pi(m_0), pi(pi(m_0)), .... That tower always reaches a fixed point pi(M) = M within about twenty levels (24, 120, 600, 3000, 15000 and 375000 are the fixed points reached from p <= 1e6). If k is at most the tower depth D, reduce n modulo m_k and walk back up with fast-doubling Fibonacci. Otherwise every level below D uses the same modulus M, so the rest is the single map T(x) = F_x mod M iterated k-D times on Z_M; precompute T for each distinct M in O(M) (it is just the Fibonacci sequence mod M) and jump k-D steps through its functional graph, then walk the D levels back up. O(D log) per query after precomputation.
problems.statement_summary: Nesting the Fibonacci function k times starting from n gives a value the task must report modulo p, for up to a hundred thousand independent queries. Both n and k reach a quintillion while the modulus p stays at or below one million, so the nested value is astronomically large and only its residue can ever be formed.
problems.review_rationale: I rule that an honest statement of the gap plus the cost model is enough, and I approve. What ships is a search record - labels, a band, a summary - so the questions that matter are whether the labels name what the real solution does and whether anything published misleads, and both now pass: the tower reduction is proved, every label names a live component, and the notes say in plain words that the verify PASS is correctness evidence only, that the fast path is not implemented, and that the limit claim rests on a design I costed at 25,593 pisano computations, 639,783 divisor probes and mean tower depth 5.29. This is also the standard the rest of the batch meets, since all ten verify scripts are small-case equivalence checks that establish nothing about time limits; requiring a working fast path here alone would be a stricter gate applied to one record because its author was candid.
issues: The performance claim remains unexecuted. My arithmetic puts the design near 2e8 elementary operations and inside the limit, but nobody has run it, and the largest thing the script executes is 710 queries of the slow variant.
M=75000 is now in the fixed-point list with the measured 2501 tail-plus-cycle beside the 12501 at 375000, matching what I found scanning 23007 moduli. The correction is accurate.

Scope limit on this approval: if the record is ever promoted past a search index, to anything implying a judge would accept it, the fast path must exist in code first. As a search record it is fine; as a solution of record it is not one yet.

problems.solution: Place vertices on a line with increasing potentials d_i and weight every edge (i,j) by d_j - d_i. Any walk then costs at least |d_end - d_start| with equality exactly for the index-increasing walks, so every increasing path is a shortest path and the count is a plain DAG count. For Bash take x_0..x_60 with d_i = i and all C(61,2) edges, giving 2^(i-1) paths to x_i, and join vertex 2 to x_(b+1) for every set bit b of A: 62 vertices and at most 1889 edges. For Chikapu take y_0..y_86 with only the edges y_(i-2)-y_i and y_(i-1)-y_i, giving Fib(i+1) paths to y_i, and join vertex 2 to the Zeckendorf terms of A: 88 vertices and 171 + at most 43 = at most 214 edges, exactly the stated cap. A = 0 is answered by the empty two-vertex graph.
problems.statement_summary: Given a value A up to a quintillion, the task builds two weighted simple undirected graphs in each of which the number of distinct shortest paths between vertex one and vertex two is exactly A. The first may use seventy-two vertices and 2525 edges, the second only eighty-eight vertices and 214 edges, and every edge weight must be a positive integer below a billion.
problems.review_rationale: I recounted the budgets myself. The potential trick is sound: with d_i increasing and edge weight d_j - d_i, any walk telescopes to at least |d_end - d_start| with equality exactly on increasing walks, so every increasing path is shortest. Bash uses 62 vertices and 1830 + at most 60 = 1890 edges against caps of 72 and 2525; Chikapu uses 88 vertices and 171 + at most 43 = 214 edges against caps of 88 and 214, i.e. exactly at the cap, and A = F(87)-1 really does need all 43 Zeckendorf terms, which is what forces Zeckendorf rather than binary for the second graph. Maximum weight is 86, far under 1e9, and all weights are positive. 219 values of A including both worst cases are recounted with exact big-integer Dijkstra path counting. Time is trivial; the only cost is emitting about 210000 output lines across 101 test cases.
issues: A = 0 is answered YES with a 2-vertex edgeless graph. The count of shortest paths between disconnected vertices is 0, so this is defensible and the output format explicitly permits M = 0, but it is a judgement call that cannot be checked offline and is the single most likely WA in this proposal.

The write-up says 'the count is a plain DAG count', but no DAG DP is ever run - the counts come from the closed forms 2^(i-1) and Fib(i+1). dp-on-dag was correctly NOT labelled; I checked for it specifically.

problems.solution: Cutting one head regrows a head, so move 1 is a no-op and the reachable moves are (H,T)->(H,T+1) for T>=1, (H,T)->(H-2,T) for H>=2 and (H,T)->(H+1,T-2) for T>=2. If a of the first, b of the second and c of the third are used then a = 2c - T and 2b = H + c, so the total 3c - T + (H+c)/2 is increasing in c and the optimum is the smallest c >= ceil(T/2) with c congruent to H mod 2. Such a plan is always orderable (all tail-growths first, then all tail-pairs, then all head-pairs), so with H, T >= 1 the answer is never -1. O(1) per test case, O(1) space.
problems.statement_summary: A knight fights a creature with H heads and T tails and may cut one head, one tail, two heads or two tails, but cutting a single head regrows a head, cutting a single tail regrows two tails, and cutting two tails grows a head. The creature dies only when both counts reach zero at once; the task is the fewest cuts, with H and T each at most 100.
problems.review_rationale: I re-derived the algebra and it holds: move 1 is a no-op, the other three give a = 2c - T, 2b = H + c, total = 3c - T + (H+c)/2 increasing in c, minimised at the smallest c >= ceil(T/2) with c congruent to H mod 2, and the plan is always orderable (all tail-growths, then all tail-pairs, then all head-pairs) so the bound is achieved. Both samples check out by hand (3,3 -> c=3 -> 9; 1,1 -> c=1 -> 3). The algebraic lower bound is independent of the verify script's LIM=400 cap, so the BFS agreement on all 10000 starts is confirmation rather than the proof. With H, T >= 1 the answer is never -1, as claimed. O(1) per test against at most 50 tests.
issues: bfs kept but with a reservation worth recording: the submitted solution is closed-form arithmetic, and BFS is an alternative route. I kept it because it is not a REJECTED alternative (unlike the batch-G pattern) - it is verified correct here on every reachable start and is plainly how most of the 1080 solvers got through - but note that a BFS solution needs an unstated cap on H and T, since two of the three effective moves increase one of the counts. The proposal does not say what bound makes that safe.

problems.solution: Count the complement: strings of length n with no occurrence of P, then subtract from 2^n (and answer 0 when |P| > n). Track the set of pattern prefixes still alive as a bitmask A, where bit l means the last l characters match P[0..l-1]; appending '1' maps A to (A<<1)|1 and appending '0' maps A to ((A & starmask)<<1)|1, and a string is rejected as soon as bit m-1 would advance. That mask is exactly the Aho-Corasick state of the up to 2^15 concrete completions of P, so the reachable state count is bounded by the trie size, at most about 30*2^15; a dictionary-keyed DP over n <= 50 characters therefore runs in O(n * states) with states under 10^6. Measured worst case over adversarial patterns was 491520 (15 times 2^15, the adversarial worst case found by review; the rigorous bound is under 983040) states.
problems.statement_summary: A pattern of at most thirty characters, each either a one or a wildcard and at least half of them ones, marks a binary string of length n as valid when some substring of the string matches the pattern position by position, with wildcards matching either bit. The task counts how many distinct valid strings of length n exist, where n is at most fifty.
problems.review_rationale: The one defect I filed is fixed and fixed correctly. The solution text now reads 491520 equals 15 times 2^15 with the rigorous bound stated as under 983040, which is verbatim my measurement, and the notes carry a dated review correction naming the adversarial pattern and admitting that the verify script does not measure state counts at all. Both numbers are the ones I produced, not rounded or silently re-derived, and the conclusion they support, about 5e7 transitions over n at most 50, is unchanged and still comfortable. Correctness was never the issue and was already settled against brute force on 500 random patterns.
issues: The state count is still unmeasured by anything in the repo; the 491520 in the text is my number, and the notes now say so rather than passing it off as the proposal's own measurement. That is the honest handling, so it is a note and not a defect.
Carried forward: at 491520 masks in one layer a dict-keyed DP costs roughly 25MB per layer, so an implementation wants a BFS over reachable masks with integer ids rather than two hash maps.
Prose nit only: 'Measured worst case over adversarial patterns was 491520 (...) states' now reads awkwardly with the parenthetical wedged between the number and its noun.

problems.solution: The happiness condition says every maximal simple path from every vertex is Hamiltonian and its far end is adjacent to the start, i.e. the graph is randomly Hamiltonian (randomly traceable). Those graphs are classified: only the cycle C_n, the complete bipartite K_{n,n} and the complete graph K_n. So for given N and M the answer is YES exactly when M = N, or N is even and M = (N/2)^2, or M = N(N-1)/2, and the corresponding graph is printed directly. Exhaustive search over all graphs on 3..6 vertices reproduces exactly this set of feasible M. O(M) per test case.
problems.statement_summary: Given a number of homes N and a required number of roads M, the task builds a simple undirected graph with exactly M edges so that from every vertex any walk that repeatedly steps to an arbitrary not yet visited neighbour, until it is stuck, has by then visited every vertex and can step straight back to its start. N is at most thirty; impossibility must be reported.
problems.review_rationale: The happiness condition really is the classical randomly-Hamiltonian (randomly traceable) property, and the Chartrand-Kronk classification into C_n, K_n and K_{n,n} is a real theorem, not a guess - the verify script independently enumerates every graph on 3 to 6 vertices, tests the property by expanding all maximal simple paths from every start, and gets exactly the predicted feasible edge counts {N, (N/2)^2 for even N, N(N-1)/2}. Constructions are re-tested for the property up to N = 8 and size-checked to N = 30. O(M) per test against N <= 30 and 30 tests. The proposal is honest that the vocabulary has no term for the classification itself, and it did not reach for hamiltonian-dp to fill the hole, which was the right restraint.
issues: After my two drops this record carries a single label. That is honest but it will under-retrieve: the actual search terms for this problem are 'hamiltonian' and 'randomly traceable', and the taxonomy has neither (hamiltonian-dp would be flatly wrong - there is no DP). This is a vocabulary gap, not a proposal defect; see notes.

problems.solution: A point strictly inside the convex hull is strictly inside any triangle containing the hull, so every point must lie on the hull boundary; and each side line of such a triangle supports the hull, so the points it can carry are exactly one face of the hull - one vertex or one whole edge. Three faces cover at most six hull vertices, so a hull with seven or more vertices is immediately NO, every edge carrying a point in its interior must itself be a chosen face, and there are at most twelve faces, hence at most 220 triples to try. A side line may be pushed inward until it supports the hull without losing any point, so the outward normal of the side carrying a face may be any direction of that face's normal cone: one fixed direction for an edge, the closed arc between the two neighbouring edge normals for a vertex. Containment is then automatic and only boundedness is left, i.e. picking d1, d2, d3 from the three disjoint cyclically ordered arcs with all three ccw gaps strictly between 0 and pi; eliminating d2, then d3, then d1 from that system over the arcs collapses it to three independent tests - the ccw gap from the END of each arc to the START of the next must be below pi - each an integer cross-then-dot test on hull edge normals. Per test case the cost is the hull, O(n log n) time and O(n) space, plus O(n) classification and O(1) face triples.
problems.statement_summary: Given up to a hundred thousand integer lattice points, possibly repeated, the question is whether some triangle of positive area has every one of those points lying on its three sides, vertices included; the triangle's own corners need not be lattice points. Many such test cases arrive in one file, with half a million points in total, and each needs a yes or no answer.
problems.review_rationale: I checked the reduction rather than the lemma, as instructed. Every step above the arc question is forced and I re-derived each: a triangle containing all points contains their hull, so an interior point can never sit on a side; each side line has the hull on one side, so its contact set is one face; three faces cover at most six hull vertices, killing a seven-gon outright, which the script confirms on an explicit 7-gon; an edge with a point strictly inside it must itself be a chosen face; and pushing a side inward until it supports the hull makes containment automatic and leaves only boundedness, which is the positive-spanning condition on the three outward normals. Both samples fall out by hand - the square is YES via a vertex-cone normal such as the line x+y=4 against x=0 and y=0, and the square plus its centre is NO on the interior point alone - and the note that three sides of a square give a gap of exactly pi is why the test must be strict. On the three-gap lemma I did not attempt a proof: necessity is immediate, since the ccw gap from d_i to d_j always contains the gap from the end of arc i to the start of arc j, and for sufficiency I tested the abstract arc problem numerically on 4000 random triples of disjoint arcs, comparing the three end-to-start tests against a grid search for a feasible choice, with zero disagreements, and otherwise I rely on the 3980-case brute force, which shares none of the solution's reasoning.
issues: Hull-size coverage in the brute-force run is lopsided: 1607 four-gons but only 105 six-gons and 16 hulls above six. Six vertices is the tightest case in the whole problem, the one where the three faces must be three alternating edges, and it is the thinnest-tested.

No scale test. The largest input run is a small random point set, while the judge allows 100000 points per case and 500000 in total. The work above the hull is O(1), so the only real cost is the hull and the input reading, but neither has been timed.

Integer margin, worth flagging for a C++ port: with coordinates to 1e9 the hull cross product reaches 8e18 against an int64 ceiling of 9.22e18, and the cross and dot tests on edge normals reach the same magnitude. Nothing overflows, but there is under 15 percent of headroom and no reduction to primitive directions on the solution path.

Vocabulary gap, same shape as the first pass recorded for jurassicjungle: the actual insight is supporting lines and normal cones, i.e. a half-plane-intersection boundedness argument, and canonical has no term for it. After the drop the record carries three fairly generic geometry labels for a 9.2 problem.
brute-force: I agree with the NO. The 220 face triples come from a set proved to have at most twelve members, so it is case enumeration of constant size, not search.

problems.solution: For a fixed left endpoint l, a word T is a subsequence of S[l..r] exactly when r >= f(l,T), the end of the greedy leftmost match of T starting at l, so each query becomes 'k-th lexicographically smallest word with f(l,.) <= r'. Sort the words once by lexicographic rank and precompute next-occurrence tables over S. Group queries by l (only |S| <= 500 distinct values); for each l compute all f(l,.) in O(total word length) with the next tables, bucket the words by that value, sweep r upward inserting words into a Fenwick tree indexed by lexicographic rank, and answer each query by descending the Fenwick tree for the k-th set position. O(|S|*(n + sum|T|) + q log n) time, O(n + q + 26|S|) space.
problems.statement_summary: Given a string of at most 500 characters, a dictionary of up to 20000 words whose lengths total 80000, and up to 300000 queries, each query names a substring by its endpoints plus an index k and asks for the k-th lexicographically smallest dictionary word that appears as a subsequence of that substring. Long answers are truncated to ten characters, and missing ones reported.
problems.review_rationale: The pivot is correct and genuinely earns the greedy label: for fixed l, word T is a subsequence of S[l..r] iff r >= the end of the greedy leftmost match, so each query becomes a k-th-smallest query over the words already inserted, answered by a Fenwick descent. Grouping by l is legitimate offline processing since |S| <= 500 caps the number of groups. I recomputed the cost: 500 groups times 8e4 total word length is 4e7 for the match phase, plus at most 500 * 2e4 Fenwick insertions at log(2e4), about 1.5e8, plus 3e5 * 15 for the queries - heavy but inside a normal limit. Verified against a naive per-query scan on 600 random cases with duplicate words retained, which matches the statement (the list of matching words is sorted, not deduplicated).
issues: The stated complexity O(|S|*(n + sum|T|) + q log n) drops a log: the Fenwick insertions cost |S| * n * log n, about 1.5e8 rather than 1e7. Still within limits, but the write-up understates the dominant term by a factor of 15.
No scale test - the largest case run is |S| = 12 with 8 words. The 1.5e8 figure is my arithmetic, not a measurement.

problems.solution: With r red piles and w white piles the line alternates, so |r-w| <= 1 and there are two orders when r = w and one otherwise. Writing F(r) for the number of compositions of R into r parts of size 1..d and C(W-1,w-1) for the compositions of W, the answer is sum_r F(r) * (2C(W-1,r-1) + C(W-1,r-2) + C(W-1,r)). Substituting F(r) = [x^R] A(x)^r with A = x + ... + x^d and summing the three binomial series collapses everything to (1+A)^{W-1} * (1+A)^2, so K = [x^R] (1 + x + ... + x^d)^{W+1} = sum_j (-1)^j C(W+1,j) C(R - j(d+1) + W, W). That is O(R+W) factorials plus O(R/(d+1)) terms; the naive per-r inclusion-exclusion would be about 7*10^10 operations at d=3.
problems.statement_summary: R boxes of red wine and W boxes of white wine are split into non-empty single-colour piles arranged in a line so that neighbouring piles always differ in colour, and every red pile holds at most d boxes while white piles are unlimited. The task is to count the distinct arrangements modulo 10^9+7, with R and W each up to one million.
problems.review_rationale: I re-derived the closed form independently and enumerated every valid line for R,W in 1..8 and d in 1..R against sum_j (-1)^j C(W+1,j) C(R-j(d+1)+W,W): zero mismatches, and both samples (3 and 6) reproduce. The collapse of the three binomial series into (1+x+...+x^d)^(W+1) is the real content and the inclusion-exclusion over the d-cap is genuinely load-bearing, as is stars-and-bars for the unbounded white compositions. O(R+W) factorial tables at 2*10^6 are comfortable.
issues: statement_summary writes the modulus as caret notation ('10^9+7') where the other eleven summaries in this batch spell magnitudes out ('one million', 'ten million'); only 3 of 71 prior A-F summaries do this, so it is a style outlier rather than a rule violation.
The proposal notes the vocabulary has no generating-function slug; that idea survives only in the tags, which is a genuine recall gap for a searcher looking for 'generating function'.

problems.solution: Count by inclusion-exclusion over the two allowed conditions. The number of length-N strings with equally many blue and red bars is C(N, N/2) for even N and zero for odd N; the number with no two adjacent blue bars is the Fibonacci value F(N+2); and the strings satisfying both have exactly N/2 blue bars, none adjacent, which is C(N/2+1, N/2) = N/2+1. So K = C(N,N/2) + F(N+2) - (N/2+1) for even N and F(N+2) for odd N. The real difficulty is the modulus: M is prime but may be far smaller than N (the samples use M=997 with N up to 10^6), so the central binomial coefficient needs Lucas' theorem digit by digit in base M. O(N + M) per dataset, O(M) space.
problems.statement_summary: A barcode is a row of N bars, each red or blue, and it is valid when the number of blue bars equals the number of red bars or no two blue bars are adjacent, or both. For up to twenty pairs of a length N up to one million and a prime modulus M up to ten million, the task is the number of valid barcodes modulo M.
problems.review_rationale: lucas-theorem is forced and I confirmed it from the constraints directly: M is any prime with 1 < M <= 10^7 while N runs to 10^6, so M can be far below N (M=2 with N=10^6 is legal) and factorial tables mod M are then useless for C(N,N/2). I independently enumerated all 2^N strings for N=1..16 against the formula C(N,N/2)+F(N+2)-(N/2+1) for even N, F(N+2) for odd: zero mismatches, and all six sample answers (2,3,5,13,34,89 mod 997) reproduce. The 'both conditions' term C(N/2+1,N/2)=N/2+1 is the inclusion-exclusion overlap and is easy to get wrong, which justifies that label.
issues: The stated 'O(N + M) per dataset, O(M) space' is conservative rather than wrong: Lucas only ever needs factorials up to min(M,N), which is at most 10^6, because when M > N the value C(N,N/2) has a single base-M digit. The honest bound is O(N + min(M,N)) time and space, ~4*10^7 over 20 datasets instead of the 2*10^8 / 40MB the claim implies.

problems.solution: Because every root-to-X path has increasing indices, the tree rooted at room 1 has parent(i) < i for every i >= 2, so room 1 has D_1 children and room i >= 2 has D_i - 1 children. Let c_1 = D_1, c_i = D_i - 1 and S_i = sum_{j<=i} c_j - (i-1), the number of still-unused child slots after rooms 1..i have been placed. The sequence is realisable exactly when sum c = N-1 (the handshake identity) and S_i >= 1 for every i < N, since room i+1 must attach to some earlier room with a free slot, and conversely any such attachment works because the parent index is automatically smaller. O(N) time and O(1) extra space.
problems.statement_summary: A network of N rooms is connected by N-1 tunnels forming a tree whose rooms are numbered so that indices strictly increase along every shortest path from room 1. Given the array of degrees, one per room, the task is to decide whether such a network can exist and print YES or NO, with N at most one thousand.
problems.review_rationale: I wrote my own enumeration of every parent array with parent<child for N=2..7, collected the achievable degree tuples, and compared against the criterion over the whole cube [1,N-1]^N: zero mismatches at every N (achievable counts 1,2,5,14,42,132). Both samples reproduce (the N=4 all-threes case fails the handshake sum, the N=8 case passes every prefix). prefix-sum is the algorithm itself - S_i = sum c_j - (i-1) is the free-slot count - and greedy carries the realisability argument that room i+1 may attach to any earlier room with a slot free. Not binary-search-answer and not tree-dp, as the solver says.
issues: Two labels is thin, but I could not find a third that is honest: the vocabulary has no slug for degree-sequence realisability or the ballot/Catalan prefix condition that actually governs this problem.

problems.solution: The ball model, pinned down by the samples: from cell (i,j) a '\\' wall rolls it down-right - it leaves by the right edge when j = N, and it is STUCK when cell (i,j+1) is '/' because the two diagonals meet in a V at their shared bottom corner; otherwise it enters (i+1,j+1) and exits the bottom at column j+1 when i = M. '/' is the mirror image. The V rule is what the last sample tests: flipping (4,4), a cell off the path, turns an exit into -1. For the queries, sqrt-decompose the ROWS. When M <= N a drop is simulated directly in O(M) = O(sqrt(MN)) steps; otherwise N < sqrt(MN) and rows are cut into blocks of B = sqrt(M/N) rows, each storing entry column -> exit column or dead, built in O(B*N). A drop walks M/B blocks and a flip rebuilds one block, both O(sqrt(M*N)). Total O(MN + Q sqrt(MN)) time, O(MN) space.
problems.statement_summary: A board of M rows and N columns holds one diagonal wall per cell, slanting either way. A ball dropped at the top of a column slides along the walls and either leaves sideways, jams between two walls, or reaches the bottom. Queries flip one wall or drop a ball, reporting its bottom exit column or minus one. Cell count and query count are each at most 100000.
problems.review_rationale: The wall physics is genuinely not in the statement - the text defers to two figures ('the ball will exit the board from the right edge:') that are absent from source_text, so no reading can be derived from the words alone. I hand-simulated the solver's model over all five sample drops and it reproduces -1, 3, 1, 4, -1 exactly, including the last -1 caused by flipping (4,4), a cell off the pre-flip path. The model is also geometrically self-consistent rather than arbitrary: a '\' in (i,j) and a '/' in (i,j+1) share a bottom corner and form a V, and the ball otherwise drops through that corner into (i+1,j+1), which makes every step advance exactly one row and bounds a naive drop at O(M). The labels survive either reading, because they describe the query structure (per-row-block entry-column to exit-column maps under point updates), not the physics.
issues: The 'solved' claim is the weakest in the batch. Five sample answers are thin evidence for a transition rule with several free choices, and the solver concedes one case - a '/\' apex, where the ball arrives at a peak - that no sample distinguishes and that it resolves by fiat ('keeping the ball's momentum'). Correctness on the real judge is unproven.

Complexity does check out under the inferred model: MN <= 10^5 so a direct drop is O(M) <= O(sqrt(MN)) when M <= N, and blocks of B = sqrt(M/N) rows give O(sqrt(MN)) ~ 316 for both drop and flip, about 3*10^7 over 10^5 queries, with O(MN) space.

problems.solution: Unlisted customer-gift pairs are worth zero, so this is the assignment problem: a maximum-weight (not necessarily perfect) matching in a bipartite graph with n customers on one side and m gifts on the other, both at most 1000. Pad the satisfaction matrix with zeros to a square, negate it and run the Jonker-Volgenant form of the Hungarian algorithm, which is O(min(n,m) * max(n,m)^2) on a dense 1000x1000 matrix and yields both the optimum and the assignment; dropping the zero-weight pairs from the printed answer is safe because weights are positive, so a zero pair never helps. Min-cost max-flow with Johnson potentials, one Dijkstra augmentation per matched pair, is the equivalent alternative. O(n*m) space.
problems.statement_summary: A company has m gifts and n loyal customers, and k survey cards each state how satisfied a given customer would be with a given gift; unlisted pairs are worth nothing. Every customer takes at most one gift and every gift goes to at most one customer. The task is to maximise the total satisfaction and print one optimal allocation, with m and n up to one thousand.
problems.review_rationale: The reduction is right and the padding argument holds: unlisted pairs are worth zero, all real weights are positive (1 <= p <= 30000), so padding to a square with zeros and dropping the zero-weight pairs from the printed assignment never loses value. The sample (11, customer 1 -> gift 2 and customer 2 -> gift 3) reproduces. hungarian-algorithm is the load-bearing claim and bipartite-matching is the honest umbrella a searcher would want.
issues: This is the tightest complexity claim in the batch. O(min(n,m)*max(n,m)^2) at n=m=1000 is 10^9 elementary operations; a tight Jonker-Volgenant or e-maxx implementation lands around 1-2s in C++, so it passes, but only because it is the intended bound and nothing asymptotically better exists for dense assignment. There is no headroom for a sloppy implementation.

problems.solution: Let cost(i,j) = min over integer v of sum_{s=i..j} |a_s - v|^k; for k=1 that is the sum of absolute deviations from the median and for k=2 the sum of squares around round(mean), both O(1) from prefix sums of a and a^2 (for k=2 test both floor and ceil of the mean). Minimising over partitions into G consecutive segments is the layered DP dp[g][j] = min_i dp[g-1][i] + cost(i+1,j). The cost obeys the quadrangle inequality, so each layer is computed by divide-and-conquer optimisation (or Knuth's monotone-opt) instead of a full scan, giving O(G*N log N) time with N=2000 and O(N) space per layer; the plain O(G*N^2) would be 8*10^9.
problems.statement_summary: A non-decreasing sequence of N heights must be cut into G blocks of consecutive positions. A block costs the minimum over all integers v of the sum of |height - v| raised to the power k, where k is one or two. The task is to report the least achievable total cost over all such partitions, with N up to two thousand and G up to N.
problems.review_rationale: I re-implemented both the plain O(G*N^2) layered DP and the divide-and-conquer-optimised version from scratch and checked the quadrangle inequality directly over all i<=p<=q<=j on 300 random sorted arrays for k=1 and k=2: zero QI violations and zero DP mismatches, so the QI genuinely survives the restriction of v to the integers, which was the one thing worth doubting. All three samples reproduce (6, 10, 3). The plain DP would be 8*10^9 at N=G=2000 so the optimisation is forced, and prefix sums of a and a^2 are what make cost(i,j) O(1).
issues: Values are safe in 64-bit: sum a^2 tops out near 2*10^15 at N=2000, a_i <= 10^6.

problems.solution: Only residues mod k matter. Let c_r be the count of residue r, base0 = sum_r floor(c_r/2)*r mod k (one element out of each equal pair), z the number of residues with odd count, and S = 2*base0 + sum of the odd residues. Mirroring is optimal for both sides: the second player can answer every pick with the partner in a fixed perfect matching, which pins the final score to base0 plus one element of each mixed pair, and the first player can take one element and then mirror. That yields an O(k) rule: z = 0 gives DRAW (the score is forced to base0 and so is the opponent's); z = 1 with odd residue r forces the first player's score to base0 + r, and the outcome is read off directly; z = 2 with residues r1, r2 is FIRST when S is nonzero and base0 + r1 or base0 + r2 vanishes, else DRAW, and SECOND is impossible for even n; z >= 3 is always a DRAW. O(n + k) per dataset.
problems.statement_summary: Two players alternately remove one number from a list of up to 1024 integers until it is empty, the first player starting, and each scores the sum of what he took. A player wins only if his own score is divisible by k while his opponent's is not; otherwise the game is drawn. Across datasets with k at most 32, report the result under optimal play.
problems.review_rationale: I verified the mirroring argument with my own from-scratch minimax rather than trusting the proposal's checker: over every residue multiset for k=2..6 and n=1..8 (4990 multisets) the O(k) closed-form rule matches exhaustive game-tree search with zero mismatches, and the structural claim that SECOND is impossible for even n holds across every even-n multiset I enumerated. On the small case the task named - k=4, [4,4,2], residues [0,0,2] - the mirroring pins base0 to 0 and forces Viet to base0+2 = 2, leaving Nam 0, so SECOND, which is the sample answer. parity-argument is load-bearing rather than decorative: the entire rule turns on z, the number of residues of odd multiplicity, and on the parity of n deciding who does the mirroring.
issues: a_i is bounded by 2^31 inclusive, which overflows a signed 32-bit read at the boundary; only residues matter so it is harmless once read as 64-bit, but it is a real input trap.
I agree with the proposal's refusal of game-dp: the exponential DP exists only inside the checker, the shipped rule is a closed form over residue counts.

problems.solution: Two cells in the same row or column must get the same real level when their virtual heights are equal and a strictly larger one when the virtual height is larger. Union-find the equal pairs (sort each row and each column and merge neighbouring equal entries), then add, between consecutive distinct values of each sorted row and column, one edge from the smaller component to the larger one; transitivity covers the rest, so the edge count stays O(mn). The minimum number of levels is the length of the longest chain, i.e. the longest path in that DAG, obtained by a topological-order DP that sets level(v) = 1 + max level over predecessors; the answer is the maximum level. O(mn log(mn)) time dominated by the sorts, O(mn) space with m*n <= 10^6.
problems.statement_summary: A floor of m by n cells carries a virtual height for every cell. Real heights must reproduce, within each row and within each column separately, both the equalities and the strict inequalities of the virtual heights, while cells in different rows and columns are unconstrained. The task is the smallest number of distinct real height levels needed, with the cell count up to one million.
problems.review_rationale: Ruling on dp-on-dag: it stays. The corpus rule asks whether the DAG is one the problem gives you rather than the DP's own state graph, and here the DAG is the precedence relation the statement itself writes down ('S_ij > S_ik if H_ij > H_ik'), contracted over the equalities. It exists before any DP is contemplated, the answer literally is its longest chain by Mirsky's theorem, and the DP is a longest-path pass over it - which is what dp-on-dag means, not a violation of it. The failure mode the rule guards against is a knapsack or grid DP whose only DAG is the memo table; that is not this. Direct precedent settles it: leetcode-maximum-strictly-increasing-cells-in-a-matrix, whose DAG is grid cells edged to strictly greater cells in the same row or column - the same construction - carries dp-on-dag + topological-sort, as does leetcode-longest-increasing-path-in-a-matrix. I also rebuilt the union-find + edge-contraction + longest-path pipeline myself and matched exhaustive level-assignment search on 400 random grids up to 3x3 with zero mismatches; the sample gives 3.
issues: sorting is more than scaffolding here: sorting each row and column is what keeps the edge count at O(mn) instead of O(mn^2), so it earns its place.
Constraints are always satisfiable (the global rank of H is a witness), so the cycle case the topological pass guards against cannot arise; that is a correct but unexercised branch, not a defect.

problems.solution: Scan the scoreboard from rank 1 downward keeping a hash set of universities already represented; a team is a winner exactly when its university is new, and the first twelve such teams get the four first, four second and four third prizes. Because only the best-placed team of each university may be awarded and ranks arrive in order, the greedy scan is forced: skipping a new university could only be replaced by a lower-ranked team of the same university, which is never allowed. At least twelve distinct universities are guaranteed, so twelve teams always exist. O(N) time and O(N) space for N<=200 lines.
problems.statement_summary: A contest scoreboard lists up to two hundred teams in finishing order, each line giving the team's university and its name. Only the highest-placed team of any university may win a prize, and exactly twelve prizes are handed out. The task is to print the twelve prize-winning teams, in scoreboard order, given that at least twelve distinct universities appear.
problems.review_rationale: A single scan with a seen-university set, N <= 200, at least twelve distinct universities guaranteed so the twelve always exist, and winners printed in scoreboard order - which I confirmed against the tail of the statement ('The winners should be listed in the same order as the input') and the 30-team sample. Both labels are the honest minimum: hash-map is the set of represented universities and simulation is this corpus's catch-all for carrying out a stated procedure, with direct precedent in atcoder-abc073-c and cses-1742, which are the same shape. I agree with the proposal's refusal of greedy: nothing is optimised, the selection is forced because only a university's top team is eligible and ranks arrive in order.
issues: The 4/4/4 prize tiers are flavour and never affect the output; a solver who tries to print prize names would be over-implementing.

problems.solution: Write S1(x) = sum_u d(u,x) and S2(x) = sum_u d(u,x)^2 inside a tree. Joining a in A to b in B leaves the two internal costs unchanged and makes every cross pair cost (dA(u,a)+1+dB(v,b))^2, so expanding the square gives cross(a,b) = M*S2A(a) + 2M*S1A(a) + N*S2B(b) + 2N*S1B(b) + 2*S1A(a)*S1B(b) + N*M. Two rerooting DP passes give S1 and S2 for every vertex of each tree in linear time. For a fixed b the a-dependent part is the line value S1A(a)*t + M*S2A(a) evaluated at t = 2M + 2*S1B(b) > 0, so building the lower convex hull of the points (S1A(a), M*S2A(a)) and querying it once per b answers everything in O(N log N + M log M) instead of the 2.5*10^9 double loop. Space O(N+M).
problems.statement_summary: Two trees of N and M computers are given; the cost of a network is the sum, over all unordered pairs of its computers, of the squared number of edges between them. Exactly one new cable must join a computer of the first tree to a computer of the second. The task is to report the minimum possible cost of the combined network, with both sizes up to fifty thousand.
problems.review_rationale: Ruling on convex-hull-trick: it is needed. I re-derived the expansion by hand - (dA(u,a)+1+dB(v,b))^2 summed over the N*M cross pairs gives M*S2A(a) + 2M*S1A(a) + N*S2B(b) + 2N*S1B(b) + 2*S1A(a)*S1B(b) + N*M - and checked it end to end on sample 1, where intA=6, intB=15 and cross(a=2,b=1)=75 sum to exactly 96. The product term 2*S1A(a)*S1B(b) is the only thing coupling the trees, and it turns the inner minimisation into 'evaluate N lines with slope S1A(a) and intercept M*S2A(a) at t = 2M + 2*S1B(b) > 0', which is precisely the hull query. The double loop is N*M = 2.5*10^9 at the stated limits, so nothing cheaper separates the trees. rerooting-dp and tree-dp both earn their place - two rerooting passes give S1 and S2 at every vertex - and they co-occur in 11 of the corpus's 14 rerooting records.
issues: Real 64-bit overflow hazard the verify script cannot see. At N=M=50000 with both trees paths, S1 reaches ~1.25*10^9 and M*S2A reaches ~2.1*10^18, so the standard hull 'bad line' cross-multiplication (c3-c1)*(m1-m2) vs (c2-c1)*(m1-m3) reaches ~2.6*10^27 and overflows signed 64-bit. An implementation needs __int128 or a division/long-double comparison. The script only tests N,M <= 7, so it would never surface this.
The worst-case cross(a,b) plus internal costs reaches roughly 8*10^18 - inside signed 64-bit but with only about ten percent headroom, and that value is computed even though it is never the minimum.

problems.solution: A rotation of p_1..p_K is the near-identity permutation rho with rho(p_i) = p_{i+1} and rho(p_K) = p_1, because the new teacher-to-class map satisfies new_pos(t) = old_pos(rho(t)). Hence after weeks w1 < w2 < ... the map is rho_{w1} o rho_{w2} o ..., and answering 'teacher d in week x' means starting from d and applying the rotations from the LATEST week at most x downwards. Sqrt-decompose the week axis into blocks of B weeks; each block stores the composition of its plans as a sparse map keyed only on the at most B*K moved teachers. A query applies its own block's plans one by one and then does a single O(1) lookup per earlier block, O(B + M/B); an insertion rebuilds one block in O(B*K). With B about sqrt(M/K) both are O(sqrt(M*K)), so O(Q sqrt(M*K)) time and O(M + Q*K) space. A segment tree fails here: rebuilding the root costs O(Q*K) per insertion.
problems.statement_summary: N teachers start in the classes of the same number and are shuffled by rotations: a plan names up to ten teachers and, from a given week on, moves each into the class the next one occupied. Plans arrive in arbitrary week order interleaved with questions asking which class a teacher holds in a given week, counting only plans issued so far. Up to one hundred thousand operations.
problems.review_rationale: I checked the permutation semantics by hand against sample 1 and the sample-2 clarification table: rotating (3,2) at week 2 sends teacher 3 to class 2 and teacher 2 to class 3, matching the table, and the solver's rho with new_pos(t) = old_pos(rho(t)) reproduces it, as do all four answers 3,2,3,1. The newest-week-first composition order is the subtle part and the proposal identifies it correctly. The sqrt bookkeeping checks out arithmetically: with B = sqrt(M/K) week-blocks, a query costs O(B + M/B) and a rebuild O(B*K), both O(sqrt(M*K)) ~ 1000, so about 10^8 over 10^5 operations. hash-map is load-bearing rather than incidental - the per-block maps must be sparse, since dense permutation arrays per block would cost (M/B)*N ~ 3*10^7 entries.
issues: The proposal's tag 'offline-structure' is wrong: queries must be answered as they arrive and each sees only the plans issued before it, so this is strictly online. Tags are outside my remit but it will mislead.
About 10^8 operations at the limits is workable but not generous; the constant on the per-block sparse lookups matters.

problems.solution: Alob's corn field must be a mirror image of Bice's rice field, so the best area is area(A intersect mirror(B)) where A and B are the parts of the polygon on the two sides of the canal; the two sides give the same answer because mirroring is an involution. Decompose the polygon (oriented counter-clockwise) into signed triangles (O, p_i, p_{i+1}) with sign s_i, so that sum_i s_i * [x in T_i] is exactly the indicator of the polygon even when it is non-convex. Clip each triangle to the half-plane to get A's pieces and clip each to the other half-plane and reflect it to get mirror(B)'s pieces - all convex with at most four vertices - and sum s_i * s_j * area of the convex-convex intersection over all pairs. O(N^2) clips, O(N) space, exact for N <= 100.
problems.statement_summary: A simple polygon of at most one hundred integer-coordinate vertices is split by a straight canal line; one brother owns everything on one side and the other brother everything on the other, and these regions may be disconnected. The two brothers plant fields that must be exact mirror images of each other across the canal. The task is the largest possible area of one brother's field.
problems.review_rationale: I attacked the modelling claim independently rather than reading their clipper. Alob's field F must satisfy F subset of A and mirror(F) subset of B, so the optimum is exactly area(A intersect mirror(B)), and the two sides agree because mirroring is an involution. I then computed that area by my own point-in-polygon Monte Carlo, with my own reflection across the canal, and got 0.0000, 9.4847 and 7.9782 against the three sample answers 0, 9.476048311178 and 8 - agreement within Monte Carlo noise and entirely independent of the proposal's code. The signed-triangle fan is what makes non-convex and disconnected pieces fall out without a polygon-boolean library, and O(N^2) clips at N <= 100 is trivial. Both labels are honest; neither is scaffolding.
issues: Two labels is thin for a 'hard' geometry problem, but the vocabulary genuinely has no slug for half-plane clipping, polygon boolean area, or reflection across a line, so I could not add anything canonical without inventing coverage.

problems.solution: Call a position a barrier when a[i] <= m. A subarray has minimum exactly m with a single copy of m iff it contains exactly one barrier and that barrier holds the value m. Since all entries are positive, the best such subarray around a given m-barrier is the maximal one: it runs from just after the previous barrier to just before the next. So scan the barrier list once and, for every barrier whose value is m, take the prefix-sum of the open span between its neighbours, keeping the maximum. O(n) time and O(n) space per dataset, n <= 10^5.
problems.statement_summary: Given an array of positive integers and a value m, the task is the largest sum of a contiguous subarray whose minimum element equals m and which contains exactly one copy of m. The array holds up to 10^5 entries, each at most 64, and always contains at least one entry equal to m; several datasets follow.
problems.review_rationale: Ran the script (0.06s): sample 12 reproduced and 3000 random cross-checks against the O(n^2) brute force clean. I re-derived the sample by hand: barriers at positions 1,3,5, the m-barrier at 5 spans positions 4..6 = 6+2+4 = 12. The reduction 'min == m with exactly one copy iff exactly one element <= m and it equals m' is exactly right, and maximal extension is optimal because all entries are positive. O(n) per dataset against n <= 1e5 and 20 datasets is trivially inside any limit.
issues: Single label after the drop, which is thin, but no second label is honest here; prefix-sum plus the barrier decomposition is the whole method.
Statement bound is written as 2^6; the summary correctly renders it as 64.

problems.solution: Straight simulation. Hold the tree with a lexicographically ordered child map per node, a cached subtree size, and a parent pointer; MKDIR and RM add or detach a node and walk to the root adjusting sizes, which is cheap because those two commands number at most 5000. UNDO is a LIFO stack of records -- undo MKDIR by detaching the created node, undo RM by re-attaching the saved subtree (kept alive, not freed), undo CD by restoring the saved current pointer -- and the stack discipline guarantees the state a record reverts to is reachable. LS needs only the first and last five keys of the ordered map; TREE needs the subtree size plus the first five pre-order lines (walk the leftmost chain) and the last five (walk the rightmost chain), so no traversal is ever materialised. O(1) to O(depth) per command.
problems.statement_summary: Simulate a directory manager over up to 10^5 commands: create, remove and enter child directories, report a directory's subtree size, list its children in lexicographic order, print its subtree in pre-order, and undo the most recent successful create, remove or change-directory command. Listings longer than ten lines show only their first and last five lines.
problems.review_rationale: The script runs clean (0.27s) and the sample 22-command transcript plus 200 random 120-command sessions against a deep-copy reference genuinely validate the tree, the subtree sizes and all three UNDO records. But the solution's central efficiency claim about TREE is false, and the script does not test it: the 'Fast' class calls preorder(cur) and materialises the whole traversal, with a comment conceding 'the real solution walks only the ends'. So the one part of this problem that is not routine is the one part left unverified. On labels all four earn their place, and design is the strongest of them.
