issues: FALSE CLAIM: 'TREE needs ... the first five pre-order lines (walk the leftmost chain) and the last five (walk the rightmost chain)'. Both halves are wrong. Counterexample built and run: root with children a (leaf) and b; b->c; c->d,e with e a leaf; d->f,g,h,i,j. Pre-order is root,a,b,c,d,f,g,h,i,j,e (11 nodes, so the >10 rule fires). True first five = root,a,b,c,d but the leftmost chain yields only root,a. True last five = g,h,i,j,e but the rightmost chain yields root,b,c,e. The pre-order predecessor of a later sibling is the last node of the previous sibling's subtree, not the parent, so no root-to-leaf chain can produce the tail.

COMPLEXITY: the method that is actually verified is O(subtree) per TREE. MKDIR+RM <= 5000 permits a depth-5000 chain, and the remaining ~95000 commands may all be TREE, giving ~4.75e8 node visits per dataset and ~9.5e9 over 20 datasets. That will not pass. The claimed chain walk would be O(depth) per TREE and equally doomed even if it were correct.

The fix is available and cheap and should be written into the solution: maintain a last-pre-order-descendant pointer per node, refreshed on the root walk MKDIR/RM already performs (<= 5000 of them, O(depth) each), then take the tail by stepping up five from it; take the head with a pre-order DFS truncated at five nodes.
The MKDIR/RM root walks are themselves up to 1.25e7 per dataset and 2.5e8 over 20 datasets. Fine, but it is the real cost and the write-up calls it 'cheap' without the arithmetic.
Acknowledged and accepted: the scraped statement is whitespace-flattened so Figure 1's indentation cannot be recovered. Output-format only, no bearing on labels or band.

problems.solution: A move replaces X by a proper divisor, and the number of prime factors with multiplicity Omega can drop to any smaller value, so each number is a nim pile of size Omega(X) and the whole list is nim -- but the last mover loses, so it is misere nim. The mover (RR) therefore loses exactly when some pile is >= 2 (a composite is present) and the xor of the Omega values is 0, or when every pile is 1 (all primes, since A > 1) and their count is odd. Sieve the primes to 10^6, run a segmented sieve on [A,B] to get Omega for each of the <= 10^5 numbers, then count subsets: a DP over the xor of composite Omegas (values < 64) combined with 2^(P-1) even/odd prime choices, plus the all-prime odd-size subsets. O((B-A) log log B + sqrt(B)) per dataset.
problems.statement_summary: Two players alternate moves on a list of distinct integers, each move replacing a chosen number by any strictly smaller divisor of it, and whoever makes the final move loses. The opponent of the first player picks the initial list freely from the integers between A and B. The task counts the winning initial lists modulo 10^9+7, with B-A at most 10^5 and B up to 10^12.
problems.review_rationale: I was asked whether all six are load-bearing and they are. Omega is the Grundy value (a proper divisor can drop the count to any smaller value, so the mex is exactly Omega), the game is misere nim, segmented sieving to 1e6 is forced by B <= 1e12, factorisation is what produces Omega, counting is the actual question, and number-theory is the taxonomy's own auto-family for sieve and factorization. I re-derived all four samples independently: [2,4] gives {2},{3} = 2; [2,5] gives 2^(P-1) = 4 all-prime odd subsets; [2,6] adds the four even-prime subsets paired with the xor-0 composite set {4,6} for 8; [2,7] gives 8+8 = 16. The misere correction is real and the samples do pin it. Script ran 4.5s clean against a full memoised multiset game search.
issues: The stated complexity 'O((B-A) log log B + sqrt(B)) per dataset' silently omits the counting step. As implemented the xor DP is O((B-A) * 64) = 6.4e6 per dataset and 6.4e8 over the permitted 100 datasets, which is the dominant term, not a rounding error. Bucketing by Omega value first (only ~39 distinct values, since 2^40 > 1e12) reduces it to O(64*64) and should be stated.

The P=0 case (a range containing no primes, reachable for large A) is handled correctly in the script via even,odd = 1,0, but no brute-force case covers it: the cross-check only ran A in [2,12], which always contains primes. Untested rather than wrong.

problems.solution: Sort all 3N scores descending. Discard the N smallest outright -- each can be parked as the weakest member of some team without touching that team's median -- and pair up the remaining top 2N in order, so the medians are the elements at sorted positions 2,4,...,2N (1-indexed) and S is their sum. Correctness by exchange: in any optimal solution the largest score is wasted as a maximum, so it should shield the largest possible median, namely the second largest, and induction repeats the argument on the rest. O(n log n) time (or O(100) counting sort, since P_i <= 100) and O(n) space.
problems.statement_summary: Given 3N students with individual scores, a coach must split them into N teams of three; a team's performance is the median of its three scores and the total is the sum over teams. The task is to report the largest achievable total. Both N and every score are at most 100, over up to twenty datasets.
problems.review_rationale: Script clean in 0.07s against exhaustive partition enumeration for N <= 3. Hand-checked the sample: 10,9,9,8,8,6 descending, drop the two smallest, medians at sorted positions 2 and 4 give 9+8 = 17. Ruling on exchange-argument at 0.6: keep. The solver's own correctness argument is literally an exchange ('the largest score is wasted as a maximum, so it should shield the largest possible median'), and this is one of the cleanest textbook instances of that proof pattern, so a searcher for the term lands somewhere useful. O(n log n), or O(100) counting sort given P_i <= 100, against N <= 100 and 20 datasets: no limit is in play.

problems.solution: Count the complement: strings of length n over 26 letters that avoid p. Build the KMP automaton of p and keep only its |p| non-accepting states; the number of avoiding strings is the row sum of T^n applied to the start state, where T[s][t] counts letters moving s to t without completing a match. |p| <= 50 and n <= 10^12, so raise the transfer matrix by binary exponentiation, about 40 squarings of a 50x50 matrix. The answer is 26^n - avoid, all arithmetic mod M. O(|p|^3 log n) time, O(|p|^2) space; M is an arbitrary modulus up to 10^12, so products need 128-bit arithmetic and no inverses may be used.
problems.statement_summary: Given a length n, a modulus M and a pattern string p of at most 50 lowercase letters, the task is to count the lowercase strings of length n that contain p somewhere as a substring, reported modulo M. The length reaches 10^12 and the modulus 10^12, so up to twenty such datasets must each be answered without enumeration.
problems.review_rationale: Script clean in 1.22s: both samples plus 120 full-enumeration cross-checks over alphabets of size 2 and 3. I re-derived the samples by hand (n=2 gives only 'ab' = 1; n=3 gives 26+26 with no overlap since s2 cannot be both a and b = 52). Complement counting on the KMP automaton restricted to its |p| non-accepting states is correct, and the transfer matrix is the right accelerator for n <= 1e12. I keep string-matching alongside kmp: the taxonomy has no family rule linking them, so it is an independent claim, and a KMP automaton is string-matching machinery even though nothing is ever matched.
issues: VERIFIED, the O(|p|^3 log n) claim does fit: 50^3 = 1.25e5 mulmods per multiply, about 60 multiplies for n = 1e12, so ~7.5e6 per dataset and ~1.5e8 128-bit mulmods over 20 datasets. Roughly 0.5-1.5s in C++, and applying the final power as a vector-by-matrix product halves it. The point about M <= 1e12 being an arbitrary modulus is right and load-bearing: products reach 1e24, so __int128 is mandatory and no inverse exists.

The big-n sanity check used p = 'abcabcabcab' (length 11), not the worst case |p| = 50, so the script never exercises the timing it claims. My own arithmetic above covers it, but the check as written does not.

problems.solution: Every channel that is actually used costs E_ij to activate plus L to push the program across it, so give each edge weight E_ij + L; the set of used channels must connect every station to some pre-installed station, and a cheapest such set is a spanning forest of the graph in which the S initial stations are contracted to a single vertex. Run Kruskal with union-find after pre-uniting the S sources, summing the accepted weights. The network is connected, so exactly N-S accepted edges (post-contraction, N-1 unions minus the S-1 free ones) always exist. O(M log M) time, O(N+M) space with M up to 10^6.
problems.statement_summary: Stations form a connected weighted network; activating the channel between two stations costs a given amount, and afterwards transmitting the L-byte program across it costs L more. The program starts installed on S given stations and must reach every station. The task is the minimum total energy, with up to 10^4 stations and 10^6 channels.
problems.review_rationale: Script clean in 0.95s against brute force over all edge subsets on 300 random connected graphs with random source sets. Hand-checked the sample: weights become 14,18,11,12,15,30, and Kruskal takes 11+12+14 = 37. The two modelling steps are both real and both correct, namely fold L into every edge because an activated channel carries the program once, and contract the S pre-installed stations into one vertex so only N-S edges are bought. graph-modeling at 0.7 earns its keep on exactly those two steps. O(M log M) with M <= 1e6 over 20 datasets is fine, and E_ij <= 1e6 even allows a counting sort if sorting were ever the bottleneck.
issues: Input volume is the practical risk rather than the algorithm: up to 2e7 edges across the 20 datasets means fast input parsing is mandatory. Worth a sentence in the solution, which currently only quotes the asymptotics.

problems.solution: For every subset S of the N <= 20 candidates, cost(S) = sum_j max_{i in S} a_ij. Write each max as a telescoping sum over prefixes: sorting topic j's students descending as v_1 >= ... >= v_N, max_{i in S} = sum_k (v_k - v_{k+1}) * [S meets the top-k set], so cost(S) = TOT - sum over (j,k) of (v_k - v_{k+1}) * [S is contained in the complement of that top-k set]. Bucket each weight on that complement mask, take one superset-sum (SOS) DP over 2^N, and cost(S) = TOT - G[S] for every subset at once. Sweep subsets by popcount for the per-K minima, so all Q queries are answered together. O(N*M + 2^N * N) time and O(2^N) space per dataset.
problems.statement_summary: A coach must teach M topics to a group of K students chosen from N candidates; teaching one topic to a group costs the largest of its members' individual times for that topic, and the group's cost is the sum over all topics. For each query value of K the task is the minimum possible total, with N at most 20 and M up to 10,000.
problems.review_rationale: Script clean in 0.04s; I also hand-checked the second sample (K=2 picks students 2 and 3 for 3+6+5 = 14, K=3 gives 3+6+9 = 18). The telescoping rewrite of max as a sum of prefix-threshold contributions, with 'S meets top-k' flipped to 'S avoids top-k' so it becomes a superset sum, is correct and is the whole idea; the naive 2^20 * 1e4 route really is dead. contribution-technique at 0.6 is undervalued rather than doubtful, since that rewrite is precisely what a searcher for the term wants to see. dynamic-programming is the taxonomy's own auto-family for sos-dp.
issues: COMPLEXITY, the one number worth stating: 2^20 * 20 = 2.1e7 per dataset, and the statement permits 100 datasets, so the nominal worst case is 2.1e9 plus a 8MB array rebuilt 100 times. What rescues it is the implied input size, since 100 datasets at N=20, M=10000 would be 2e7 integers, on the order of a 100MB input file. The write-up quotes per-dataset cost only and never confronts the multiplier.

problems.solution: Preemptive scheduling of n jobs on m identical machines with release times and deadlines, which is feasible iff a transportation-style flow saturates. Cut the timeline at the sorted distinct r_i and d_i values (at most 400 boundaries, so <= 399 intervals) and build source -> job i (cap p_i) -> interval k (cap len_k, present only when [t_k,t_k+1) lies inside [r_i,d_i]) -> sink (cap m*len_k); a schedule exists iff max flow equals sum p_i, because any schedule induces such a flow and any flow can be realised. Realise it with McNaughton's wrap-around inside each interval: lay the per-job amounts end to end along a strip of length m*len_k and cut it into m printer rows, which never splits a job across two rows at the same instant since each amount is <= len_k. Dinic on ~600 nodes and ~80000 edges per dataset.
problems.statement_summary: Up to 200 files, each with a page count, a release time and a deadline, must be printed on m identical printers; printing may be interrupted and resumed on any printer, but a file may occupy only one printer at a time and each printer prints one page at a time. The task is to decide feasibility and, when feasible, emit an explicit schedule.
problems.review_rationale: Best-verified item in the batch: the script (0.06s) checks the compressed flow against a unit-time-slot flow AND against an exhaustive slot-by-slot DFS on 300 tiny instances, then re-validates every emitted schedule against all four statement rules, and its check() asserts r <= a < b <= d, which is the corrected constraint. The compressed-equals-unit-slot claim is sound on its own terms too: aggregating a unit-slot flow satisfies the caps (len_k, m*len_k) trivially, and the converse is exactly McNaughton, since each per-job amount is <= len_k so its wrapped piece ends at a+off and never overlaps its own pre-wrap piece in time. dinic at 0.5 is too low, not wrong: with flow up to sum p_i = 6e6 the algorithm choice is forced, since Ford-Fulkerson or Edmonds-Karp would not finish.
issues: STATEMENT DEFECT CONFIRMED. The output spec prints the period constraint as d_i <= x < y <= r_i, which is unsatisfiable because d_i - r_i >= p_i >= 1 puts r_i strictly below d_i. The sample settles it: file 1 has r=2, d=7 and its first period is '2 4', which needs r_i <= x < y <= d_i. I re-validated the whole sample schedule by hand (per-file page totals 4/3/3/5, every period inside its window, no file on two printers at once, and printers 1 and 2 each fully non-overlapping), and dataset 2 is correctly NO since 15 pages cannot fit 9 time units on one printer.

Dinic's theoretical worst case on this network is not argued anywhere. Augmenting paths lengthen by 2 per phase up to O(min(n, intervals)) = O(200) phases at O(V*E) = ~4.8e7 each, which is nowhere near the limit on paper; it is fine in practice on a three-layer transportation network, but the write-up should say so rather than quote node and edge counts and stop.

OUTPUT VOLUME, unexamined and explicitly capped by the statement at 10MB. McNaughton can split a job twice per interval, so up to 2 * 399 * 200 = ~160k lines per dataset, and 25 datasets could approach the cap unless consecutive periods of the same job on the same printer across an interval boundary are merged. Neither the solution nor the script mentions the cap.

problems.solution: Let cap[i] be the water volume held when the surface stands exactly at the brim of wall i. Water enters at the left, so at that moment tank t (t <= i) is at level max(H_t..H_i), and every drowned wall t < i additionally carries a unit-wide column of water from H_t up to the level on its right. Building cap[] left to right with a monotonic stack of pools -- push each new tank, pop and raise every block whose level is below the new wall's height, merging widths (the wall itself joins the pool as a width-1 block at its own height) -- gives all N values in O(N) amortised, and cap is strictly increasing. A query K then answers count{ i : cap[i] < K } by binary search, strictly, because a reservoir filled exactly to a brim has not yet spilled. O(N + Q log N) time, O(N) space.
problems.statement_summary: A reservoir cross-section is divided into tanks by N unit-thick walls at given positions and heights; water pours in at the top left and spills rightwards over the walls. For each of up to 10^5 query volumes the task is the index of the last wall the water flows over, or zero. Positions reach 10^9 and volumes 10^15.
problems.review_rationale: Script clean in 0.05s, O(N) stack against the O(N^2) definitional formula on 2000 inputs, and it also asserts cap strictly increasing every time, which is what licenses the lookup. I rebuilt all four caps by hand and got [2,13,16,18]: cap[2] = 5 for tank 1 at level 5, plus 3 for the column on drowned wall 1, plus 5 for tank 2. The solver's refusal of binary-search-answer is correct and I endorse it, since the binary search is an ordinary lower_bound in a precomputed increasing array with no feasibility predicate anywhere.
issues: The solver undersells its own evidence. It says the sample pins two of the three fitted choices; I checked and it pins all three. Setting tank 1's width to L_1 - 1 = 0 instead of L_1 gives caps [0,8,11,13] and answers 3 for K=13 instead of 1, and dropping the water column standing on a drowned wall gives caps [2,10,13,15] and answers 2 for K=13 instead of 1. Both readings are excluded by the single sample.
Confidences are inverted: binary-search at 0.9 over monotonic-stack at 0.85, when the stack is the entire problem and the binary search is one lower_bound call. Recommend swapping them.

caps_def is an independent implementation but not an independent physical model; it encodes the same three assumptions. The sample excludes the alternatives I could construct, so I am satisfied, but this remains modelling fitted to one example.

problems.solution: At water level h a ball of radius r either floats, displacing exactly its own weight w * (4/3)pi r^3, or sits on the bottom submerged to depth min(h, 2r), displacing the spherical cap pi t^2 (3r - t)/3; the physical displacement is the smaller of the two, which makes displaced(h) continuous and non-decreasing. The level therefore solves W*L*h - sum_i displaced_i(h) = V, monotone in h, so binary search h over [0, D] (about 100 iterations for 10^-9) and clamp at D when even h = D leaves net volume below V. O(n log(1/eps)) time, O(n) space, n <= 1000.
problems.statement_summary: A rectangular pool of given width, length and depth receives a fixed volume of water together with n spheres, each with a radius and a specific weight; heavier balls rest on the bottom while lighter ones float, and both displace water by Archimedes' principle. The task is the resulting water level, capped at the pool depth, to within 10^-4 error.
problems.review_rationale: Ruling on binary-search-answer at 0.65: KEEP, and raise it. The predicate is monotone because f(h) = W*L*h - sum displaced_i(h) is literally the water volume standing at level h and each displaced_i is non-decreasing, and the feasibility test is where all the work sits, namely the float-versus-grounded split resolved as min(cap(min(h,2r)), w*(4/3)pi r^3) plus the spherical cap volume. That min is genuinely elegant and I checked it holds in both directions: a sinker has w*V > V_sphere >= cap(min(h,2r)) so the cap always wins, and a floater sitting in shallow water is correctly grounded because cap(h) < w*V there. Keeping binary-search alongside is the project's own family implication, not redundancy. Script ran 12.3s, both samples to 1e-8, and the 2.4e-5 worst gap against the dense scan is exactly that scan's own resolution of D/200000, so it is not error.
issues: STATEMENT DEFECT CONFIRMED, and I confirmed it from the sample rather than taking it on trust. The statement writes 'two positive real numbers r_i and w_i indicating the specific weight and radius', so the symbol order and the prose order disagree. Sample dataset 2 decides it: reading 0.8 as the radius gives (5 + (4/3)pi*0.512)/4 = 1.786165145, matching the expected 1.78616514621 exactly, while reading 0.8 as the specific weight gives (5 + 0.8*(4/3)pi)/4 = 2.088, which clamps to D = 2 and would print 2.0. Input is radius then specific weight; the prose is wrong. Note that sample dataset 1 is useless for this, since both of its values are 1.0.

Monotonicity is assumed, not established, and the constraints do not guarantee it. With n <= 1000, r <= 2 and W*L as small as 4, the balls' total horizontal cross-section can far exceed the pool's, and since the statement declares 'no interaction among the n balls' such an input is formally legal and would make f decrease. Physically impossible, so presumably absent from the test data, but the solution asserts monotonicity as a fact and it is really an assumption about the data.
The dense scan is an independent check of the same equation, not of the physics. Correctly acknowledged by the solver.

problems.solution: The price is the number of digits 6 or 8 occurring in the multiples of 8 up to n, plus the digits of n itself when n is not a multiple of 8 (when it is, it was already counted once). Count the first part with a digit DP over the <= 19 digits of n whose state is (position, value mod 8, tight, started), returning both how many numbers each branch completes and how many lucky digits they contribute; a digit contributes its own count times the number of completions below it. O(19 * 8 * 10) per query, O(1) extra space -- fast enough for 100000 queries, and n <= 10^18 rules out any enumeration.
problems.statement_summary: A staircase of n steps has its number engraved on every step whose index is a multiple of eight and on the final step; each engraved digit 6 or 8 costs a precious stone, and the tour price is the number of such digits. For a given n, as large as 10^18, the task is that price, for up to 100,000 independent queries.
problems.review_rationale: Script clean in 0.26s against enumeration for n <= 300 and 400 random n up to 30000. I hand-verified every sample: n=9 gives 8 alone for 1; n=32 gives 8,16,24,32 for 2; n=56 gives 8,16,24,32,40,48,56 for 4 with 56 engraved once and not twice; n=18 gives 8,16 for 2 plus the digit 8 of the final step for 3. The (position, value mod 8, tight, started) state is right, leading zeros are correctly excluded from both the count and the lucky tally, and the double-count guard for n divisible by 8 is exactly what sample n=56 is there to catch. f(10^18) = 4.81e17 is the right order, since ~1.25e17 multiples of 8 at roughly 3.6 lucky digits each lands near 4.5e17.
issues: Per-query cost is ~19*8*10 transitions, so ~1.5e8 over the permitted 100000 queries. Fine in C++ but only if the memo is keyed per query rather than rebuilt with allocation each time. The solver notes a closed form exists because divisibility by 8 depends only on the last three digits; that is true and would be materially faster, but the digit DP as specified does fit.

problems.solution: Every empty cell uses exactly two of its four sides, and a side is used iff the neighbour across it uses the opposite side, so a valid layout is exactly a subgraph of the empty-cell grid graph in which every vertex has degree 2. The cost is 0 unless the two sides are opposite (left+right costs h, up+down costs v), i.e. the cost of sending 1 or 2 units horizontally out of a cell is convex (0 then h), which is expressible as two parallel unit edges. Colour the grid like a checkerboard: source -> black cell (cap 2) -> Hport/Vport through the (1,0),(1,cost) pairs -> the matching port of each horizontal/vertical neighbour (cap 1) -> mirrored white gadget -> sink. Feasible iff the flow saturates 2 * #black, which needs #black = #white; the min-cost flow value is the answer. O(V*E*flow) min-cost flow on ~1200 nodes and ~3200 edges with flow <= 800.
problems.statement_summary: Every empty cell of a grid up to 20 by 20 must receive exactly one pipe: a straight horizontal one, a straight vertical one, or a freely rotatable curved one, and the pipe ends must join so that all water circulates in closed loops with no leaks. Straight pipes carry per-cell costs; the task is the cheapest valid layout, or a report that none exists.
problems.review_rationale: I checked the reduction by hand on the 3x4 sample as asked, and it holds. Independently of the code: the degree-2 characterisation is right because every pipe uses exactly two sides and a side is usable only if the neighbour across it reciprocates, so valid layouts are exactly the degree-2 subgraphs of the empty-cell grid graph, which are exactly disjoint unions of cycles. On sample 2 every cell has grid-degree 2 or has its choice forced by neighbours, giving the single 10-cycle (0,0)-(0,1)-(0,2)-(1,2)-(1,3)-(2,3)-(2,2)-(2,1)-(2,0)-(1,0), whose straight cells cost h(0,1)=2 plus v(1,0)=5 plus h(2,1)=1 plus h(2,2)=2 = 10, matching. I then re-derived the same 10 through the gadget from port loads alone: black (2,2) sends 2 horizontally for h=2, white (0,1) receives 2 horizontally for h=2, white (1,0) receives 2 vertically for v=5, white (2,1) receives 2 horizontally for h=1, every other cell splits 1 and 1 and pays nothing. Sample 3 is NO for the right reason, 5 black cells against 4 white. Script 7.9s clean against exhaustive six-side-pair enumeration on 119 grids.
issues: The convexity justification is stated loosely and should be corrected, because as written it is not true. Per-cell cost as a function of horizontal degree alone is (v, 0, h) for degrees (0, 1, 2), whose increments are -v then +h, so it is convex but not monotone and cannot be modelled by two non-negative parallel edges. What the gadget actually does, and what is correct, is per-PORT convexity: each of the H and V ports charges 0 for its first unit and h or v for its second, which yields h, 0, v for horizontal degree 2, 1, 0 respectively, with every cost non-negative. The code is right; the sentence explaining it is not.
'flow <= 800' is wrong; the flow value is 2 * #black <= 400 on a 20x20 grid.

Cost bound unexamined: with up to 100 datasets of 20x20, ~400 augmentations each over ~3200 edges, this is on the order of 1e9 operations in total. Costs are non-negative so Dijkstra with potentials is available and a blocking-flow MCMF pushes many units per phase, but the write-up quotes O(V*E*flow) without ever multiplying by the dataset count.

Feasibility needs #black == #white, which is necessary but the solution presents it as if it were also sufficient before the flow. The code gets this right (it checks parity first, then requires saturation); the prose runs the two together.

problems.solution: Colours are only ever copied, so the set of live colours can shrink but never grow: a necessary condition is that every colour of t already occurs in s (and for n = 1, s = t). For a connected graph with n >= 2 that is also sufficient, and the witness is built in two phases. Phase A repairs the colour multiset: while some colour occurs fewer times than t needs, take a vertex whose colour is in surplus, BFS to the nearest vertex whose colour is in deficit, and walk the surplus one edge at a time toward it, each move being a single vertex copying a neighbour; only surplus vertices are overwritten, so no needed colour is ever lost, and each unit of deficit costs at most one shortest path. Phase B permutes: with the multiset correct, match holders to targets and realise that permutation by adjacent swaps on a spanning tree, peeling leaves in reverse DFS order so the working part stays connected - a swap is one legal step because the update is simultaneous and both endpoints read the other's old colour. O(n^3) work, O(n) steps per repair, comfortably inside 20000 steps.
problems.statement_summary: Each vertex of a connected undirected graph carries one of k colours, and in one step every vertex simultaneously either keeps its colour or takes the colour of a neighbour. Given a starting and a target colouring on at most a hundred vertices with at most a hundred colours, the task is to decide reachability and, when reachable, print a witness sequence of at most twenty thousand steps.
problems.review_rationale: The feasibility criterion is right and the proposal identifies the real trap - the update is simultaneous, so a 3-cycle of colours is reachable in one step while any one-vertex-at-a-time argument would call it Impossible - and it was checked exhaustively over every connected graph on 2..4 vertices with k<=3 against every (s,t) pair, which is the correct shape of evidence for a reachability claim. Sample 2 (n=1, s!=t) is the Impossible branch. The cost model fits: O(n^3) at n<=100 is nothing, and the output is at most 20001 lines of 100 integers. The step budget is the only limit at risk and it is tight rather than comfortable.
issues: Step budget has no proof, only measurement: phase A is bounded by n units of deficit times a shortest path (<=9900) and phase B by adjacent swaps along tree paths (<=9900), summing to ~19800 against a hard 20000. The worst observed was 3614, and the two phases plausibly cannot both peak (a large deficit implies surplus is everywhere, so repair paths are short), but nothing rules it out.

tags contains 'simulation' while the notes explicitly argue the problem is not simulation ('nothing is simulated forward, the sequence is constructed'). tags are indexed, so this contradicts the write-up - remove it.

problems.solution: Reconstructing the (unavailable) figure from the samples: the corridor is 0 <= y <= w, a shaft of width l rises above the ceiling gap from (0,w) to (l,w), door A is hinged at (0,w) and points (cos A, -sin A) into the corridor, and door B is hinged on a corridor wall further right so its tip stands l*sin B above that wall. A disc gets through a planar passage exactly when every bottleneck pair of obstacles is at least 2r apart, and here there are only two bottlenecks: entering the corridor past door A, which is the distance from the far shaft corner (l,w) to the door segment - l*sin A while the foot of the perpendicular lies on the door (A <= pi/2), else l, the plain shaft width - and squeezing past door B, a gap of w - l*sin B. So the answer is min(R, l*sin(min(A,pi/2))/2, (w - l*sin B)/2), O(1) per scenario, O(1) space.
problems.statement_summary: A circle of radius R starts far above a corridor of width w and must reach a point far to the right inside it, avoiding the walls and two hinged doors of length l, with the door length never exceeding the corridor width. For each of up to ten thousand scenarios giving the two door angles in radians, the task reports the largest shrunken radius that still gets through.
problems.review_rationale: The closed form reproduces all four sample answers exactly (3*sin(1.0472)=2.598079885, l/2=3, (w-l)/2=1, and 0 for the closed door) and O(1) per scenario against T <= 10^4 is trivially inside the limit, so neither samples nor complexity are the problem. Two of the three terms are pinned by the text rather than the missing figure: A=0 giving 0 and A=pi giving l/2 force the ceiling gap to be exactly l with door A hinged at one edge, and 'l <= w so that door B will never hit the opposite side of the wall' confirms door B is hinged on a corridor wall with tip height l*sin B, gap w - l*sin B. What is not pinned is the separation of the two doors, and I verified the risk is real rather than theoretical: the verify script hard-codes door B at x=20 and computes clearances from the same reconstructed layout it is testing, so its grid search is circular and cannot detect a missing door-A-to-door-B term.
issues: status 'solved' overstates a solution the proposer rates 0.55 and explicitly calls a reconstruction; the bounded fix is to fetch the figure from the Kattis problem page and confirm door B's x-offset, after which this is either approved as-is or gains one clearance term.

The verify script's grid check is not independent - clearance() is built from the reconstructed layout, so formula-vs-grid agreement proves only self-consistency. Its agreement is also only to 0.06 at grid step 0.1.
The proposal's note says the verify script 'takes a few minutes'; it runs in 3.1s, matching verify-run.txt. Stale note.

Labels are safe either way - it is plane geometry under both layouts - but one label is thin. I found no honest second: binary-search-answer is correctly refused (the route taken is closed form, and T=10^4 wants O(1)), and adding it would be the batch-G flaw.

problems.solution: Clip each moving rectangle to the scene [0,W]x[0,H] (objects that drift off the picture stop counting - that is why waiting is said to help) and let f(t) be the area of the union. Sweeping in x, f(t) = sum over vertical strips of (strip width) times (measure of the union of the active y-intervals). While no two of the 2N+2 relevant x-coordinates - the object edges plus the clip lines 0 and W - swap, and likewise for y, each strip's active set and the merge pattern of its y-intervals are frozen, so both factors are linear in t and f is a single quadratic on that interval. Every order change is the root of a linear equation, so there are O(N^2) event times; sort them, and on each interval fit the quadratic from three samples and test its vertex along with the endpoints. With N <= 50 that is about 10^4 intervals times an O(N^2) union-area evaluation, and the minimum is exact rather than sampled. O(N^4) time overall, O(N^2) space.
problems.statement_summary: Up to fifty axis-aligned rectangles move at constant velocities across a photographed scene of given width and height. For any moment within the next E seconds a picture may be taken, and the task is the smallest possible area of the scene covered by the union of those rectangles at the chosen moment, reported to within a millionth relative error.
problems.review_rationale: I checked the piecewise-quadratic claim rather than taking it: within an interval where no two of the 2N+2 x-coordinates and no two y-coordinates swap, each strip's active set and the merge pattern of its y-intervals are frozen, so strip width and covered y-length are each linear in t and the union area is one quadratic - and crucially the clip lines 0, W, 0, H are included among the coordinates, so an object drifting off the scene is itself an event rather than a discontinuity. Sample 2's answer 300 at t=5.75 (the small rectangle swallowed by the large one) is the case that would break a sampler. The explicit refusal of ternary-search is correct and important: the area is genuinely not unimodal in t. Space is O(N^2) event times, trivial.
issues: 'O(N^4)' understates the constant. The event count is C(2N+2,2) over two axes, so ~10^4 intervals at N=50, and each needs three union-area evaluations of ~5*10^3 operations even with a pre-sorted merge - roughly 2*10^8 elementary operations. Fine in C++, but it is not the 6*10^6 that N^4 suggests, and a per-strip resort would multiply it again.
The verify script only ever builds 1 to 6 objects, so nothing in this batch exercises N=50; the runtime claim is unmeasured.

Fitting the quadratic from three samples is ill-conditioned on very short intervals; harmless here only because f is Lipschitz in t, so the missed vertex costs O(interval length) and stays far inside the 1e-6 relative tolerance.
