problems.solution: Building i is visible exactly when h_i exceeds every earlier height, so a prefix is summarised by (running maximum H, number visible so far) and the DP is over those states. With H fixed, an invisible building is cheapest at h_i = min(p_i, H), costing c_i*max(0, p_i - H) and leaving H alone (and it is illegal while H = 0, since heights are positive, which is why building 1 is always visible); a visible building may take any height above H and becomes the new maximum. The trap is that a visible building is NOT always best at max(p_i, H+1): lowering it below its preferred height can be worth it so a later cheap building can still clear it, so the candidate heights are p_j + d for |d| <= n - O(n^2) values - and the visible transition is evaluated with a prefix minimum over the running-maximum axis. That gives O(n^2 * n^2) = O(n^4) time at n = 70 and O(n^3) memory rolled to two layers; the answer is the cheapest state with at least k visible.
problems.statement_summary: Positive integer heights must be chosen for n buildings standing in a row, where building i costs its cost factor times the distance from its preferred height. A building is visible from the tram at position zero when it is strictly taller than every building before it, and the task is the cheapest assignment making at least k of the n buildings visible.
problems.review_rationale: I verified the sample by hand: heights 5,6,4,9,6 cost 0+6+0+0+0=6 with buildings 1, 2 and 4 visible, matching the stated answer of 6. The state (running maximum, number visible so far) is the right summary of a prefix, and the proposal caught the actual trap with a brute force rather than by assertion - P=[4,4,1,1], C=[1,3,4,4], k=2 costs 1 only by LOWERING building 1 below its preferred height, which kills the natural h_i=max(p_i,H+1) greedy DP and forces candidate heights p_j+d with d of both signs. Limits fit: n<=70 gives O(n^2) candidate heights, O(n^4)=2.4e7 states with O(1) transitions via the prefix minimum, and O(n^3) memory rolled to two layers is a few megabytes. Costs reach 70*1e9*1000, so the accumulator must be 64-bit.
issues: The candidate set {p_j + d : |d| <= n} is the load-bearing claim and it is only validated against brute force at n<=5, where |d|<=n is barely exercised. A targeted case with a long chain of forced shifts would be worth more than 300 more random n<=5 cases.
Two labels survive, which is thin for a 7.1; I looked for a third and rejected dp-optimization (a prefix minimum is not what that term retrieves) rather than pad the list.

problems.solution: A subgraph of a tree that is a perfect k-ary tree is just a connected vertex subset, and since k >= 2 its root is the unique vertex of degree k (internal nodes have degree k+1, leaves degree 1), so counting each candidate at its root counts it exactly once. Let down[h][v][p] be the number of perfect k-ary subtrees of height h rooted at v that avoid the neighbour p; then down[h][v][p] is the elementary symmetric polynomial of degree k in {down[h-1][u][v] : u in N(v), u != p}, because the root must pick exactly k of its available neighbours and each must carry a height h-1 perfect subtree. The answer is N (the single vertices, h = 0) plus the sum over h >= 1 and over v of e_k taken over all of v's neighbours. Heights stop at log_k N (<= 17 for k = 2, N = 10^5), and evaluating e_k with one element removed for every directed edge is done with prefix/suffix symmetric polynomials rather than division, giving O(N k log_k N) time and O(N k) space modulo 10^9+7.
problems.statement_summary: A tree with up to a hundred thousand labelled nodes is given along with a value k between two and five. The task is to count, modulo one billion and seven, how many subgraphs of the tree are perfect k-ary trees, meaning they can be rooted so that every internal node has exactly k children and all leaves sit at equal depth.
problems.review_rationale: The counting argument is airtight and I checked the part that decides it: in a perfect k-ary tree with k>=2 the root has degree k, internal nodes k+1 and leaves 1, so with k>=2 the root is the unique degree-k vertex and counting at the root double-counts nothing; height 0 is the separate N singletons. The sample verifies exactly - 4 singletons plus e_2 at each of the two internal vertices of the 4-path gives 6. Limits are comfortable: heights stop at log_k N <= 17, the per-edge exclude-one elementary symmetric polynomial is done with prefix/suffix products for O(N k log_k N) ~ 3*10^6 at N=1e5, k=2, and O(Nk) space with rolled layers. The performance trap the proposal names is the real one: a star makes the naive exclude-one recomputation O(deg^2), and division is unavailable because a child value can be 0 mod p, so prefix/suffix is not optional.
issues: rerooting-dp is the one debatable keep. The DP is indexed by directed edge from the start rather than rooted-then-rerooted, so it is not the two-pass idiom - but exclude-one-neighbour aggregation over every directed edge is the thing rerooting searchers are looking for, so I kept it rather than drop a genuinely useful retrieval term.
modular-arithmetic survives on a real argument rather than as scaffolding: the impossibility of dividing by a zero residue is what forces the prefix/suffix construction.

problems.solution: Write each number as the exponent pair (a,b); gcd is the componentwise minimum and lcm the componentwise maximum, and the two exponents are combined by the same op, so values must be compared as 2^a*3^b. Any combining tree with k gcd-ops and N-1-k lcm-ops whose root is an lcm is exactly a partition of the N items into m = N-k blocks, taking the componentwise min of each block and the componentwise max across blocks (dually, the smallest outcome is m = k+1 blocks with max inside and min on top) - a brute force over all trees confirmed this family is complete. If m >= 3 two singleton blocks can carry the global maximum of a and of b independently, so the answer is the global componentwise max; m = 1 is the global componentwise min; only m = 2 needs work, and there the optimum is either a singleton block against the rest or the split induced by an a-threshold, both swept with prefix/suffix componentwise minima after one sort. O(N log N) time, O(N) space, and every scenario k is answered in O(1) from those precomputed arrays.
problems.statement_summary: Each of N numbers is given as two raised to some power times three raised to some power, and repeatedly two numbers are replaced by either their greatest common divisor or their least common multiple until a single number remains. For every count k of gcd merges from zero up to N-1, the task reports the largest and the smallest final value obtainable.
problems.review_rationale: Checked the model against the sample by hand: with numbers (0,0),(1,2),(2,0) the three scenarios give (2,2)/(2,2), (1,2)/(0,0), (0,0)/(0,0), matching. I re-derived the m=2 case independently: writing a=max(min_a over B1, min_a over B2) and b likewise, either both coordinates come from one block (best is a singleton block, covered) or they split, in which case every item with a_i < A is forced into B2 and B = min{b_i : a_i < A} - exactly the sorted a-threshold sweep the proposal describes, so the candidate family is complete. N <= 50000 against O(N log N) time and O(N) space with O(1) per scenario is far inside any limit; exponents <= 1000 mean values must be compared as exponent pairs or big integers, which the proposal states.
issues: Two of five labels are decoration; after the drops the entry is gcd + number-theory + sorting, which is the right shape.
'sorting' is kept only because the sorted a-order IS the m=2 algorithm, not because a sort is performed somewhere.

problems.solution: Within a round the worker's height never decreases, so the cells he touches at level h form one contiguous interval of the level-h occupied columns; hence a round is a root-to-node path in the tree whose nodes are the maximal intervals of {i : H_i >= h} for each h, i.e. the Cartesian tree of H by minimum (children of an interval are the pieces it splits into above its minimum). Every round entering a node's subtree places at most M of that subtree's cells and ends inside one child, so rounds(v) >= max(sum of rounds over children, ceil(cells(v)/M)), where cells(v) counts the subtree from v's base level upward; because cells shrink as the level rises, the whole chain of equal intervals collapses to its bottom level. That bound is achievable, so the answer is the sum of f(root) over the maximal runs of positive H, computed in O(N) time and O(N) space with a monotonic stack building the Cartesian tree.
problems.statement_summary: A worker must place a required number of horizontal bamboos in each of the columns of a vertical grid, building from the ground upward. In one round he carries at most M bamboos, starts at ground level, and may only move left, right or up, onto bamboos already there or ones he places, never descending while loaded. The task is the fewest rounds.
problems.review_rationale: The statement reading is right, which was the thing to check on a 5.1 that only 15 teams solved: 'you cannot go down while carrying' plus 'once you finish placing, you go down' makes height non-decreasing inside a round, so the columns touched at each level form one contiguous interval and, since higher levels' intervals nest inside lower ones, a round is a root-to-node path of the Cartesian tree of H by minimum. I re-checked both samples against f(v)=max(sum of children, ceil(cells(v)/M)): sample 1 gives max(1+1, ceil(8/4))=2 and sample 2 gives max(3, ceil(8/10))=3, and the ceil term alone would wrongly answer 1 on sample 2. O(N) time and space at N <= 1e5 with H_i <= 1e5 is comfortable, and cells(v) must be accumulated as a 64-bit sum (up to 1e10). Re-checked after the rework: the summary now reads 'a required number of horizontal bamboos in each of the columns', carries no subscripts or other markup, and is 63 words, so the one blocker I raised is cleared and this is approved. The bare M for the carrying capacity is consistent with the plain variable names I accepted in the teamup and peaktram summaries, and the source hash and the four patterns are unchanged, so nothing else in my review moves.
issues: RESOLVED: the LaTeX subscripts are gone from statement_summary (63 words, no markup); this was the only thing holding the entry.

Achievability of the max(...) bound is only checked by BFS on N<=5, H<=4, M<=5 (294 shapes). That is the half of the argument that can be wrong and it has no proof; worth one hand-written larger case where a round must serve a node's own block and a child in the same trip.
Kattis scores this 5.1 but only 15 teams solved it; I band it hard - the difficulty is entirely in reading the movement rule, not in the O(N) code.

problems.solution: A cut whose heaviest crossing edge is at most W is precisely a union of connected components of the graph keeping only edges of weight > W, and those components are the components of the MAXIMUM spanning tree after deleting its edges of weight <= W. So the only candidate thresholds are the n-1 maximum-spanning-tree weights, and at threshold W the best denominator is best(W) = the largest subset sum of the component sizes not exceeding floor(n/2) (a union heavier than half is replaced by its complement); the answer is min over tree weights w of w / best(w). Unions of several components genuinely beat single components, so the subset sum is real work: build the max spanning tree with Kruskal and union-find in O(m log m), then sweep thresholds upward and evaluate the subset sum with a bitset over floor(n/2) bits, grouping equal component sizes. Pruning keeps it inside the strict limit: the running answer only falls, best(W) <= floor(n/2) means the sweep can stop once w/floor(n/2) reaches the current answer, a component larger than n/2 makes best = n - that size outright, and the greedy descending fit gives a valid lower bound (>= floor(n/2) - maxsize + 1) that tightens the answer cheaply before any exact DP is run.
problems.statement_summary: A connected weighted undirected graph with up to fourteen thousand vertices and thirty thousand edges is given. The slimness of a cut is the largest weight among the edges crossing it divided by the number of vertices on the smaller side, and the task is to report the minimum slimness over all cuts, within a hundred-millionth relative error under a strict time limit.
problems.review_rationale: I re-derived the characterisation and it holds in both directions: a cut with heaviest crossing edge <= W has no edge of weight > W crossing it, so S is a union of components of the graph restricted to edges of weight > W, and conversely. Restricting candidate thresholds to the n-1 maximum-spanning-tree weights is also safe, since the component structure of the >W subgraph only changes at those weights and any non-tree W rounds down to one of them without increasing w/best(w); every value considered is achievable-or-worse, so the minimum is exact. The sample's 4/3 checks out. I disagree with the proposal's pessimism about the running time: the two costs are in tension, because d distinct component sizes with multiplicity m satisfy m*d^2/2 ~ n, so binary-split shift-ORs per threshold peak around 200 regardless of the split, giving ~3*10^8 word operations over all 14000 thresholds at n=14000 even with no pruning at all.
issues: The worst case the proposal feared - many distinct sizes AND best(W) below floor(n/2) - is hard to build, because many distinct sizes make the attainable subset sums dense and dense sums hit floor(n/2) exactly, which fires the stop rule immediately. An adversary needs all sizes sharing a factor that misses floor(n/2) (e.g. odd n with all-even components), and that forces the distinct-size count down. Worth recording, since it converts an unproven pruning into a bounded argument.
The 'strict time limit' still means the bitset and the equal-size grouping are mandatory, not optimisations; a plain per-threshold subset sum over components is 10^10-ish and will time out.

Not added, deliberately: the threshold sweep is the level structure of a Kruskal reconstruction tree over the maximum spanning tree, but the solution never builds one, so labelling kruskal-reconstruction-tree would name a route not taken.

problems.solution: A closed tour exists for every board except a single line of 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8 or 9 squares and the 2x2 board; exhaustive search over the move graph confirms exactly that list (a lone row of 6 to 9 squares dies because two of its cells are forced onto the same pair of neighbours and close a short cycle). Every other board is built by tiling: cut the rows and the columns into parts of size 2 to 5 so that no 2x2 block ever appears (a part of size 2 is used only when that whole side has length 2), give each block its own closed tour, and splice the next block into the growing cycle by deleting an edge (u,v) of the cycle whose two ends lie in the neighbouring block, deleting an edge (u',v') of the block's own cycle, and adding (u,u') and (v,v'); the blocks are side by side so a legal pair of edges always exists. A single row with M >= 10 is done the same way from a base of 10 to 14 columns plus appended blocks of five, 1x5 being the only short line that works. The block tours are constant-size, so the construction is O(NM) time and O(NM) space, which is the size of the output.
problems.statement_summary: On a grid of N rows and M columns, each at most two hundred, the task is to visit every square exactly once in a cyclic order where consecutive squares, including the last and the first, are at Manhattan distance two or three, never one and never more. Any such tour may be reported, or a statement that none exists.
problems.review_rationale: This is the best-verified proposal in the batch and I could not break it. Both samples pass (the emitted 2x3 tour differs from the statement's but is legal, which the problem allows, and 1x1 is -1 because a tour needs length at least two). I read the script rather than trusting the claims, and the logic is airtight in a way the write-up undersells: impossibility only ever has to be proved for tiny boards, and the 16 claimed-impossible pairs are all at most 9 cells, while every other board is proved possible by producing a tour and validating it cell by cell - so exhaustive DFS and construction between them close the case with no gap. I re-derived the two interesting entries by hand: 1x4 dies because columns 2 and 3 have degree one in the move graph, 1x6 dies because the four degree-two cells force three edges onto column 3, and 1x5 survives as the 5-cycle 1-3-5-2-4. O(NM) time and space is the output size at NM <= 40000, so limits are not in question. I also ran the construction well past what the script covers - all 6384 legal boards up to 80x80 - and every one built and validated, with the no-2x2-block invariant holding throughout (only 15 gadgets are ever used, none of them 2x2).
issues: The script's docstring is stale and contradicts the notes: it says exhaustive DFS on N*M <= 14 plus 1xM to M <= 16, while the code does N*M <= 16, every line to 20 cells, and five extras. The notes are the accurate ones - I ran it and got exactly the 63 small boards and 560 constructed boards they claim, in 1.0s. Same class of stale-note defect as doors, which claimed minutes for a 3s script.

The solution prose says 'the blocks are side by side so a legal pair of edges always exists', but special_tour does not rely on that - it has a fallback that retries the merge against the block above, and asserts only if both fail. I instrumented it over every board to 60x60: 346270 merges, zero primary failures, so the claim holds empirically and the fallback is untested dead code. Worth saying out loud, because the prose asserts something stronger than the implementation is willing to bet on.

Boards between 25x25 and 199x199 are only spot-checked by the script (nine of them). The risk is genuinely low because parts() reduces every side to threes plus one final part of 3, 4 or 5, giving only nine structural classes, all of which appear below 24x24 - and my 80x80 sweep found nothing - but the coverage claim should be stated as structural rather than exhaustive.

One pattern label survives, which is thin for a 7.5. That is a vocabulary gap rather than a labelling failure: there is no canonical term for splicing two disjoint cycles through a pair of nearby edges, nor for tiling a board with constant-size gadgets, and the proposal says so itself. Recall is carried by the tags (construction, grid, manhattan, hamiltonian-cycle) and by the statement text, which is the right place for statement vocabulary.
Unlike doors, the verification here is genuinely independent: check() recomputes every Manhattan step against the raw definition rather than against the model that produced the tour.

problems.solution: Build the Aho-Corasick automaton of the N taboo strings over the binary alphabet and mark a state bad if it ends a taboo string or if any state on its suffix-link chain does (propagated in BFS order). A binary string avoids every taboo string exactly when the walk it traces from the root never enters a bad state, so the clue length is the longest walk in the automaton restricted to good states. If any good state reachable from the root lies on a cycle of good states the clue is unbounded and the answer is -1; this is detected by the same DFS that computes best[u] = 1 + max over characters of best[goto(u,c)] over good successors. Rebuilding the string is a greedy walk from the root taking '0' whenever it still attains best[u], which gives the lexicographically smallest among the longest. O(sum of lengths) states, transitions, time and space.
problems.statement_summary: Given up to fifteen thousand binary taboo strings whose lengths total at most two hundred thousand, the task is to find the longest binary string that contains none of them as a substring, printing -1 when arbitrarily long such strings exist. Among all longest answers, the lexicographically smallest one must be reported.
problems.review_rationale: Both samples check out by hand: with 00, 01, 10, 110, 111 taboo the only good walks give 11, and with 00, 01, 10 the all-ones walk cycles so -1 is right. The reduction is exactly right and the two edge cases the proposal names are the ones that sink naive attempts - terminal-ness must be inherited along suffix links, and with both single characters taboo the answer is the empty string rather than -1, since taboo strings are non-empty so the root is good. Sizes are comfortable: sum of lengths <= 2e5 gives <= 2e5+1 states over a binary alphabet, linear time and space, and the printed answer is bounded by the number of good states. I agree with the refusal of dp-on-dag on the stronger ground the proposal only half-states: the good-state graph is not a DAG at all in the -1 case, which is the whole point of the cycle test.
issues: Label list was the longest in the batch at eight; two were decoration.
The greedy reconstruction must compare best[] over the '0' branch including the case best=0 (empty answer), where the output is an empty line - easy to print as nothing at all or as -1 by mistake.

problems.solution: The pairwise nested-or-disjoint condition makes the classes a laminar family, so inclusion gives a forest; the parent of a set is found in O(sum|S_i|) by processing sets in decreasing size and keeping, per skill, the deepest set seen so far (equal-size sets are disjoint, so ties are harmless). Covering the set S_v needs either one player of class v or one cover of every child of v, and the children route is available only when their sizes add up to |S_v| (otherwise the gap skills are uncoverable inside v). Hence g(v) = cnt[v] + min over children g(c) when the children tile S_v, else cnt[v]; a team needs one cover per root, so the answer is min over roots g(root), and 0 when the maximal sets fail to cover all n skills. The teaming is emitted by zipping the first g covers of each child, O(n + m + sum|S_i| + p) time and space.
problems.statement_summary: Given n skills and m character classes whose skill sets are pairwise nested or disjoint, plus p players of known classes, a team is a set of players whose classes together cover every skill and each player joins at most one team. The task asks for the maximum number of teams that can be formed simultaneously and one such teaming.
problems.review_rationale: I re-derived the recursion: a cover of S_v either is one class-v player or must cover every child's set from that child's subtree, since every class contained in S_v is v itself or lies in exactly one child's subtree; hence the child route needs the children to tile S_v and the count is cnt[v] plus the bottleneck child, which is what the proposal has. The answer is min over roots and 0 when the maximal sets miss a skill, correct because a team must cover all n skills. Parent-finding in O(sum|S_i|) by decreasing size is sound - anything already stamped on a shared skill is a strict superset. With sum|S_i| <= 5e5, m,p <= 3e5 the O(n+m+p+sum|S_i|) time and space is not close to any limit, and the printed teaming is bounded by p players.
issues: constructive-algorithm is kept but is the weakest survivor: the teaming must genuinely be emitted, though the construction is a by-product of the count rather than the difficulty.
Nothing checks the 'children tile S_v' test at scale; sizes must be compared with the parent's |S_v|, and a node with a single proper child must fall through to cnt[v] only.

problems.solution: Problem p is forced first, so if its estimate exceeds 300 the team solves nothing and the answer is '0 0'. Otherwise the clock starts at t[p]; among the remaining problems, solving them in increasing order of estimate maximises how many fit in the 300 minutes (the classic shortest-job-first exchange argument), and for a fixed set the same increasing order also minimises the penalty because the penalty is the sum of prefix sums, which weights the i-th smallest by (k-i+1). The largest feasible set is also the set of smallest estimates, so one greedy pass answers both parts. O(N log N) time, O(N) space.
problems.statement_summary: A team faces N problems, at most thirteen, with distinct estimated solving times, and insists on attempting a designated problem first before working on the rest in any order. The contest lasts three hundred minutes and a problem counts only if it is finished by then. The task is to report the largest number of problems solved and, among orders achieving that, the smallest total ICPC penalty time.
problems.review_rationale: verify_acm2.py passes all four samples and 2000 exhaustive-permutation fuzz cases in 0.1s, and I re-derived the forced-first-problem case by hand (t[p] above 300 yields '0 0', which sample 3 exercises). Sorting at most 13 estimates is O(N log N) against a 300-minute budget, so time and space are non-issues. Both labels are load-bearing: the sort by estimate is the algorithm, since the same increasing order simultaneously maximises the count and minimises the penalty, which is a sum of prefix sums.

problems.solution: Every minion is an interval [L,U] of acceptable temperatures and a room is one temperature, so this is the minimum piercing (stabbing) set of N intervals: pick the fewest points so that every interval contains one. Sort the intervals by right endpoint and sweep: whenever the next interval starts after the last point placed, place a new point at that interval's right endpoint. That point is the latest position that still stabs the current interval, so it dominates every other choice, giving optimality by the standard exchange argument. O(N log N) time, O(N) space, trivial for N <= 100.
problems.statement_summary: A company must house N minions, at most a hundred of them, in as few rooms as possible. Each room is set to a single temperature, and every minion accepts only temperatures inside a personal closed interval whose endpoints lie between one and twice N. The task is to report the minimum number of distinct temperatures needed so that every minion can be assigned to a room it likes.
problems.review_rationale: verify_airconditioned.py passes both samples and 3000 fuzz cases in 0.1s. With N at most 100 and endpoints inside 1 to 2N, any polynomial method fits, so the only live question is labelling. interval-scheduling survives my attack: the minimum piercing set equals the maximum set of pairwise-disjoint intervals by duality and is computed by the identical earliest-right-endpoint greedy, so it names the technique and not a merely adjacent topic.

problems.solution: Group each fruit's boxes into i maximal runs and knock out runs of length >= 2 by inclusion-exclusion; equivalently read off the Smirnov generating function 1/(1 - x/(1+x) - y/(1+y) - z/(1+z)). That gives ans = sum over i,j,k of (-1)^(A-i+C-j+M-k) C(A-1,i-1) C(C-1,j-1) C(M-1,k-1) (i+j+k)!/(i!j!k!), which is O(A*C*M) as written. Factor it: with a_i = (-1)^(A-i)C(A-1,i-1)/i! and likewise for the other two fruits, ans = sum_n n!*(a*c*m)[n], a single triple convolution of polynomials of degree <= 2*10^5. Two NTT products (three NTT primes plus CRT, or Kronecker substitution) give O(n log n) time and O(n) space with n = A+C+M <= 6*10^5.
problems.statement_summary: Boxes of three fruit types, namely A apples, C cherries and M mangos with each count between one and two hundred thousand, must be shipped in a single line so that no two neighbouring boxes hold the same fruit. Two shipments differ when some position carries a different fruit. The task is to count the valid orders modulo one billion and seven.
problems.review_rationale: fft is needed at the limits, not decoration. With A, C and M each up to 200000 the unregrouped triple sum is O(A*C*M) near 8e15, and the standard alternative of inserting one colour at a time while tracking bad adjacencies is O(n^2) near 1.6e11, so the degree-200000 triple convolution genuinely has to go through NTT at n = A+C+M up to 600000. verify_applescherriesmangos.py passes all three samples, matches exhaustive enumeration for every A, C, M up to 4, and separately confirms the convolution regrouping reproduces the triple sum exactly; it ran 34.5s. Space is O(n) words, well inside any limit.
issues: 1e9+7 is not an NTT-friendly modulus, so the three-prime-plus-CRT route the proposal names would earn chinese-remainder-theorem; I left the label off because the Kronecker-substitution alternative the proposal also names avoids CRT entirely, which makes the label implementation-dependent rather than intrinsic

problems.solution: Binary search on R with the arc-cover decision test. If some disk of radius R covers K points, sliding its centre away from them until the farthest covered point sits at distance exactly R shows there is a witness centre on the circle C_i of radius R about some input point i. For a centre on C_i, another point j is covered exactly on an arc of half-width acos(d(i,j)/(2R)) around the direction i->j, so collect those arcs for all j within 2R, sweep their endpoints and compare 1 + max overlap with K. Feasibility is bounded by U = min_i d_{K-1}(i): R* lies in [U/2, U], and a square of side U/2 holds fewer than K points, so only O(K) points lie within 2R of any i. That makes a decision O(N K log K) and is exactly why the input promises K <= 20 or N <= 5000. O(N) space.
problems.statement_summary: Up to a hundred thousand cats sit at distinct integer points of a plane, and one camera placed anywhere sees every cat within its visual range R. Find the smallest R letting the camera see at least K cats, where K is at most two hundred and, in every test, at most twenty unless the number of cats is at most five thousand.
problems.review_rationale: Correctness holds up: the sample passes and 150 random point sets match exhaustive pair-and-triple circle enumeration, and binary-search-answer is genuinely earned because the arc-cover feasibility test is the entire content of the problem. The time limit is the failure. Kattis gives this problem 11s CPU and 1024MB; I measured the real cost driver, the number of arcs built per decision, exactly on worst-case-shaped inputs, and the clustered cases put even an optimised C++ implementation roughly 1.5x to 2.5x over. The proposal offers no performance evidence at all, because verify_cameramakers.py's decide() is an O(N^2) loop over every j and is run only on point sets of at most 7 points.
issues: Measured arcs per decision (exact, grid-based, over all N points): N=100000 K=20 uniform gives 2.3e6, but the same N and K with 19-point clumps on a lattice of spacing U gives 1.67e7 - the mean neighbour count within 2R rises from 23 to 167. N=5000 K=200 uniform gives 2.7e6, clumped gives 1.29e7 (mean 2579, max 4178).

Cost of one decision in the clumped N=100000 K=20 case is about 1.67e7 acos evaluations plus about 3.34e7 event slots sorted in per-point chunks, on the order of 1s in optimised C++. Reaching 1e-3 absolute precision on a bracket of width U/2 needs about 21 to 23 halvings, so even crediting an early exit on every true decision the total lands near 15s to 26s against the 11s limit.

The proposal's stated worry is misdirected. It fears the neighbour bound 'degenerates to O(N)' in the N<=5000 K<=200 regime, but the packing argument caps the count well below N there (measured 2579, not 5000). The actual blow-up is clustering, which multiplies the neighbour count by about 5x to 7x in BOTH regimes and is not mentioned anywhere in the proposal.

Clustered inputs are precisely what stresses the O(K)-neighbour bound the whole solution rests on, so a judge data set for a problem whose constraint clause reads 'K <= 20 or N <= 5000' is likely to contain them.

Computing U as the minimum over i of the distance to the (K-1)-st nearest neighbour needs a spatial index at N=100000; the verify script does it by O(N^2 log N) brute force, so that step is unevidenced too. I confirmed separately that a uniform grid makes it cheap, so this is a gap in the evidence rather than a second bottleneck.

problems.solution: Maintain the ingredients as disjoint sets. The invariant is that every group is either a single never-used ingredient or exactly the contents of one live cauldron, because brewing merges precisely the groups it consumes into the new cauldron. A recipe S is therefore brewable iff every group meeting S is contained in S, which is checked by collecting the distinct roots of S and testing that their sizes sum to |S|; if so, union them all and count the brew. Union-find with union by size gives O(sum(M) * alpha) time and O(max ingredient id) space, well inside sum(M) <= 500000.
problems.statement_summary: Recipes numbered one through N are considered in order, and a recipe is brewed exactly when its ingredient list can be assembled from ingredients never used before together with whole earlier cauldrons, each of which may be poured in only if all of its contents appear in that recipe. Brewing is compulsory whenever it is possible. With ingredient lists totalling half a million entries, count how many recipes get brewed.
problems.review_rationale: I re-derived the invariant and it holds: every disjoint-set group is either an unused singleton ingredient or exactly the contents of one live cauldron, so a recipe S is brewable iff every group meeting S is contained in S, and the size-sum test decides that exactly, because the groups are disjoint and together cover S. verify_control.py passes both samples and 4000 fuzz cases against the literal simulation in 0.1s. With the sum of M at most 500000 and ingredient ids at most 500000, the union-find is O(sum M * alpha) time in about 500001 words of space, comfortably inside the limits.

problems.solution: A strictly convex lattice polygon is exactly a cyclic sequence of edge vectors with pairwise distinct directions summing to zero, so take primitive vectors (gcd 1, which forces distinct directions and hence no three collinear vertices), sort them by angle and take prefix sums. To make the sum vanish, use antipodal pairs {v,-v}; for odd N start from the three vectors (1,0),(0,1),(-1,-1), which already sum to zero, and pair up the rest. Greedily take the pairs of smallest L1 norm, because the bounding box is exactly sum|a_i| by sum|b_i| over the chosen representatives. O(N log N) after an O(N) sieve of primitive vectors, O(N) space.
problems.statement_summary: Given N between three and four hundred thousand, the task is to output any convex polygon with exactly N vertices, every vertex at a lattice point with both coordinates between zero and forty million, all vertices distinct and no three of them collinear. Any valid polygon is accepted, in any vertex order, and the output is large enough that fast printing matters.
problems.review_rationale: The construction is sound: edge vectors with pairwise distinct directions summing to zero give a strictly convex lattice polygon, primitivity forces the distinct directions and rules out three collinear vertices, antipodal pairs handle even N and the seed (1,0),(0,1),(-1,-1) handles odd N. verify_convex.py ran 1.7s and measured the bounding box actually used, worst case 38251233 by 38225960 at N=399999 against the 4e7 cap, i.e. 4.4% of slack, confirming the coordinate budget is the real difficulty. gcd survives the attack for the reason just given, and sorting is load-bearing twice, once by angle to close the polygon and once by norm to fit the box.

problems.solution: The configuration (cell, program counter) determines everything and the step map is deterministic, so the state graph is a functional graph on at most N*N*L <= 8*10^6 nodes. Walk it with first-visit timestamps until a state repeats, which exposes the rho's cycle, then replay exactly one lap and collect the cells actually entered. That block B repeats forever; if it is empty the robot has stopped moving and the trail is finite, so print 1. Otherwise the tail is B repeated, whose minimal period divides |B|, so take p = |B| - failure[|B|] from the KMP prefix function and answer p when p divides |B|, else |B|. O(N^2 * L) time and space.
problems.statement_summary: A robot starts on an empty cell of an N by N grid whose border is solid wall and repeats a program of at most N characters drawn from left, right, up and down, skipping any step that would enter a wall. Its trail records only the cells it enters. Print one if that trail is finite, otherwise the length of its eventual repeating block.
problems.review_rationale: verify_cool1.py passes all four samples and 1500 random grids cross-checked against a long direct simulation, in 2.9s. I traced samples 1, 2 and 4 by hand and the state-graph framing is right: the step map on (cell, program counter) is deterministic, so the rho's cycle is found in at most N*N*L states, about 8e6 at N=200. kmp is genuine and not decorative - the cycle gives a period of the trail but not necessarily the minimal one, and the prefix function is what reduces the repeated block to its primitive period, so the label names a step that is actually executed.
issues: The proposal's justification for kmp cites sample 1 as the case where the reduction bites, but sample 1's state cycle is a single pass producing the two-cell block, which is already primitive, so the prefix function is a no-op there. The step is still correct and still needed in general; only the cited example is wrong.

The proposal says 'O(N^2 * L) time and space' without a byte figure. At N=200 that is 8e6 states of first-visit timestamps, about 32MB at 4 bytes, plus a prefix-function array over a block that can itself reach 8e6, another 32MB. That fits a typical 1GB Kattis limit but is worth stating explicitly rather than hiding inside an asymptotic.

problems.solution: Only a hundred colours exist, so the multiset of colours in a subtree can be summarised by a 100-bit parity mask, and the number of magical colours is its popcount. Flatten the tree with a DFS euler tour so each subtree is a contiguous index range, and keep the per-position masks in a Fenwick tree whose operation is XOR; XOR is its own inverse, so the range mask is prefix(tout) XOR prefix(tin-1). A recolour is one point XOR of two bits. O((N+Q) log N) operations on two 64-bit words, O(N) space, for N <= 3*10^5 and Q <= 10^6.
problems.statement_summary: A rooted tree of up to three hundred thousand nodes has every node coloured with one of a hundred colours, and a colour is called magical for a subtree when it occurs an odd number of times inside it. Up to a million operations arrive in order, each either recolouring one node or asking how many colours are currently magical in the subtree of a given node.
problems.review_rationale: verify_magicallights.py passes both samples and 400 random tree and operation mixes in under 0.1s. The reduction checks out: 100 colours fit a 128-bit parity mask in two words, XOR is its own inverse so a Fenwick tree over XOR supports both the point update and the prefix-XOR difference that gives a subtree range. At Q up to 1e6 and N up to 3e5 that is about 3.6e7 word-XORs and roughly 5MB of Fenwick, so time and space are not close to the limits. parity-argument survives: odd-occurrence equals XOR parity is the reduction, not a restatement.
issues: euler-tour and tree-flattening name the same step twice - one DFS producing tin/tout so each subtree is a contiguous range. I am NOT dropping either, because this is a corpus-wide convention rather than a batch J defect: 7 of the 8 euler-tour uses in the corpus co-occur with tree-flattening, and the nearest neighbours of this problem (cses-1137, cses-1138, codeforces-1076-e, leetcode-shortest-path-in-a-weighted-tree) all carry the pair. Dropping it here alone would make this problem inconsistent with its own neighbours. Flagging for a corpus-wide decision instead - see notes.

problems.solution: The cost M + K/M over divisors M of K falls on (0, sqrt K] and rises after, and the two candidates M and K/M give the same cost, so the answer comes from the largest divisor of K that is at most isqrt(K). K has roughly 1200 bits and up to 10^10 divisors, so meet in the middle: split the prime powers into two groups with divisor counts as equal as possible (greedy over the factors e_i+1, each at most 101, so each side is about sqrt(D)), enumerate each group's divisors, sort the second, and for every d1 binary-search the largest d2 with d1*d2 <= isqrt(K). The cost is reduced mod 1e9+7 with a modular inverse for K/M, which is safe since every prime factor is below the modulus. O(sqrt(D) log sqrt(D)) big-integer comparisons, O(sqrt(D)) space.
problems.statement_summary: A customer needs exactly K bytes of storage bought as identical servers of M bytes each, where M must divide K, and the price is M dollars of base cost plus one dollar per server. K arrives as a string of two-digit prime factors, up to three hundred and fifty of them, and may have ten billion divisors. Report the least cost modulo one billion and seven.
problems.review_rationale: Confirmed the binary search is a sorted-list lookup and NOT binary-search-answer: the script bisects a sorted array of second-half divisors for the largest d2 with d1*d2 at most isqrt(K); there is no monotone feasibility predicate on the answer, so the proposal's own note is right and binary-search is the correct slug. The operation count and arithmetic size also hold up under my own adversarial inputs, with margin to spare. The reduction to the largest divisor at most sqrt(K) is correct because M and K/M cost the same and f(M) = M + K/M is unimodal, and the modular inverse is safe because every prime factor is under 100 and so under the modulus.
issues: I attacked the operation count with inputs the script's own stress test does not reach. The script stresses only a 645-bit K (its primes are 2, 3, 5, 7, ...), while the real worst case for bignum width is large primes: 97^100 * 89^100 * 83^100 plus 13 more distinct primes is 313 factors, 2019 bits, 8.44e9 divisors, sides 81608 and 103424 - and it still solves in 0.09s in CPython. The script's own 346-factor 5.41e10-divisor case (already over the problem's 1e10 cap) takes 0.23s, and a 10-prime 1e10-divisor case with sides 100000 each takes 0.05s. C++ will be far faster, so the limits are met with a wide margin.

The docstring's 'O(sqrt(D) log sqrt(D)) big-integer comparisons' undercounts slightly: d1*d2 is a multiplication, not a comparison. The script sidesteps this by computing S // d1 once per d1 and then bisecting on plain comparisons, which is the right implementation and is what makes the measured times so small - worth stating, since a literal multiply-per-comparison reading would be about 1.7e6 multiplications of 1000-to-2000-bit numbers.

problems.solution: Executives get consecutive blocks from the front, so the answer is the maximum number of parts in a left-to-right split of the array whose block sums are non-decreasing. Run a prefix DP that stores, for every prefix, the Pareto-best pair (largest number of blocks, and the smallest last-block sum attaining it): dp[i] takes the best j < i with pre[i]-pre[j] >= last[j], breaking ties toward the largest j so the new last block is as small as possible. More blocks never hurt and a smaller last block never hurts, so one pair per prefix suffices; the fuzz confirms this against exhaustive splits. O(N^2) time with N <= 3000, O(N) space.
problems.statement_summary: N briefcases, each holding some bananas, are handed out in order to executives ranked by evilness: each executive receives a positive number of the lowest-numbered briefcases still available. A more evil executive must end up with at least as many bananas as every less evil one. With N up to three thousand, the task is to maximise how many executives can be rewarded.
problems.review_rationale: verify_mububa.py passes both samples and 4000 random plus 600 skewed cases against all 2^(n-1) splits for n up to 12, in 1.9s. That exhaustive check is the right target, because the one thing worth attacking here is the Pareto claim that a single (most blocks, smallest last-block sum) pair per prefix suffices - I could not produce a clean proof that a shorter split with a much smaller last block never wins later, so the exhaustive fuzz is doing real work. O(N^2) at N up to 3000 is 9e6 operations in O(N) space, nowhere near the limits. dp-on-dag is correctly excluded: the only DAG is the DP's own prefix-to-prefix state graph, not a graph the problem supplies.
issues: The Pareto-dominance argument is asserted rather than proved ('more blocks never hurt and a smaller last block never hurts'), and its support is exhaustive enumeration only up to n=12. The claim is very likely right and the skewed-value fuzz is the correct stress, but a reader should know the justification is empirical, not a proof.
